# SI Units & Thermodynamics SI units, gas law derivations, latent heat, specific heat capacity, and laws of thermodynamics Système International (SI) defines seven base units from which all other units are derived. In anaesthesia, the most commonly encountered derived units are the (pressure = N/m²), (energy = N·m), and (power = J/s). Temperature in gas calculations must always be in (K = °C + 273.15). 1 atmosphere = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg ≈ 1033 cmH₂O = 14.7 psi = 1.013 bar . (The cmH₂O equivalence comes from P = ρgh with ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².) Understanding these conversions is essential for interpreting arterial blood gases, ventilator settings, and gas cylinder pressures. The SI unit of pressure is the Pascal, though mmHg and cmH₂O remain in widespread clinical use. Celsius scale defines 0 °C as the freezing point and 100 °C as the boiling point of water at 1 atmosphere. The Fahrenheit scale sets water's freezing point at 32 °F and boiling at 212 °F. Conversions: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9 . Normal body temperature (37 °C = 98.6 °F). Kelvin scale is the SI unit of temperature and is an — its zero point (0 K = −273.15 °C) represents the theoretical minimum where molecular motion ceases. The Kelvin scale has no negative values , which is why it must be used in all gas law calculations. Using Celsius in PV = nRT would give nonsensical results because a "doubling" of temperature from 10 °C to 20 °C is not a doubling of absolute temperature (283 K to 293 K is only a 3.5% increase). Why Kelvin matters for gas laws: Charles' law states V ∝ T (at constant P). If you plot volume against temperature in °C and extrapolate to zero volume, the line crosses the x-axis at −273.15 °C — this is absolute zero. Spirometry readings taken at room temperature (20 °C = 293 K) corrected to body temperature (37 °C = 310 K) increase by 310/293 = 5.8%. Quick Conversion Reference Celsius → Kelvin: K = °C + 273.15 (e.g., 37 °C = 310.15 K) Celsius → Fahrenheit: °F = (°C × 1.8) + 32 (e.g., 37 °C = 98.6 °F) Fahrenheit → Celsius: °C = (°F − 32) / 1.8 (e.g., 104 °F = 40 °C) Key landmarks: 0 °C = 273 K = 32 °F | 37 °C = 310 K = 98.6 °F | 100 °C = 373 K = 212 °F zeroth law of thermodynamics : the measuring device must reach thermal equilibrium with the tissue being measured. Core temperature is best reflected by the pulmonary artery catheter (gold standard), distal oesophageal probe (lower third, near the heart), and nasopharyngeal probe Tympanic membrane thermometry uses infrared detection (its proximity to the internal carotid artery allows a rapid, non-invasive estimate of core brain temperature) Peripheral sites (axillary, skin) are 0.5–1 °C lower than core. The core-peripheral gradient Thermometry Devices — Physical Principles Seebeck effect — voltage at junction of two dissimilar metals (copper–constantan). Fast, used in PA catheters Semiconductor whose resistance falls exponentially with temperature (NTC). Sensitive, used in oesophageal/rectal probes RTD (platinum): Resistance increases linearly with temperature. Very accurate laboratory standard — slower than thermistors Infrared tympanic: Detects IR radiation whose intensity is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law: j* = σT⁴); peak wavelength shifts with T per Wien's displacement law. Non-contact, <2 s, but accuracy affected by cerumen/positioning Liquid crystal: Cholesteric crystals change colour with T. Forehead strips — convenient but inaccurate (±1–2 °C) Perioperative temperature management: Hypothermia (<36 °C) prolongs neuromuscular blockade, reduces MAC, impairs platelet function, increases wound infection rates, and triggers shivering (↑VO₂ 200–400%). Current UK guidance is NICE (Perioperative care in adults, 2020), which superseded the earlier CG65 (2008/2016). NG180 defines inadvertent perioperative hypothermia as a core temperature <36.0 °C, requires induction not to begin unless the patient is ≥36.0 °C, and instructs that forced-air warming devices be set to maintain a patient temperature of at least 36.5 °C . The superseded CG65 is retained on the NICE site for archival reference only ideal gas equation PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J/mol/K) describes a hypothetical gas with no intermolecular forces and negligible molecular volume. All individual gas laws are special cases when certain variables are held constant: Boyle's law Charles' law (constant P, n → V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂), and Gay-Lussac's law (constant V, n → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). Avogadro's hypothesis states that equal volumes of all ideal gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules (V ∝ n). Avogadro's constant (6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) is the number of elementary entities in one mole, and it follows that one mole of any ideal gas at STP occupies 22.4 L . Clinical example: a size E oxygen cylinder contains about 680 L of gas ≈ 30 mol (680 ÷ 22.4), so the available volume and duration at a given flow can be calculated from moles; the same logic underlies vaporiser output calculations Dalton's law (total pressure = sum of partial pressures) underpins the alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = FiO₂(P − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/RQ. Henry's law (amount dissolved ∝ partial pressure × solubility) explains nitrogen narcosis, decompression sickness, and blood gas analysis. Real gases and the van der Waals equation molecules have negligible volume compared with the container, and (2) there are no intermolecular forces . At high pressures the molecules' own volume becomes significant, and at low temperatures (near liquefaction) attractive intermolecular (van der Waals) forces become significant. The van der Waals equation (P + a(n/V)²)(V − nb) = nRT , where the constant corrects the available volume for the finite size of the molecules. For one mole (n = 1), this reduces to (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT Critical Temperature and Pressure Critical temperature is the temperature above which a substance cannot be liquefied, no matter how much pressure is applied. Critical pressure is the pressure required to liquefy a substance at its critical temperature. Important critical temperatures are water 374 °C nitrous oxide 36.5 °C , and oxygen −118 °C liquid under pressure . Oxygen's critical temperature is far below room temperature, so oxygen is stored as a compressed gas. Its pressure falls progressively as gas is used, making the pressure gauge a useful estimate of contents in accordance with Boyle's law Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K. Water has an exceptionally high c ( 4.18 kJ/kg/K ), providing thermal stability to the body (60% water) and making water an effective warming/cooling medium. Q = m × c × ΔT calculates the heat energy transferred. Latent heat is the energy required for a phase change at constant temperature. The latent heat of vaporisation of water ( 2260 kJ/kg ) is very large — evaporation is therefore extremely effective at cooling, explaining why evaporative loss is the dominant mechanism of intraoperative heat loss from exposed surgical surfaces, and why sweating is so effective. zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium as transitive — if two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is the fundamental basis of temperature measurement. first law (conservation of energy: ΔU = Q − W) states energy cannot be created or destroyed. In an adiabatic expansion against a piston Joule–Thomson effect , is the temperature change seen when a gas undergoes expansion (throttling) through a valve or orifice with no work done and no heat exchange — the mechanism operating in cylinder pressure regulators and cryotherapy probes . The Joule-Thomson coefficient (μ is the change in temperature per unit change in pressure at constant enthalpy, and its sign determines the direction of the effect: most gases (except hydrogen and helium) have a positive μ at room temperature and cool on expansion , while hydrogen and helium have a negative μ and warm unless pre-cooled below their inversion temperature. Clinical applications and risks. carries high-pressure N₂O or CO₂ down a narrow tube to its tip, where the gas passes through a very small orifice (a throttle). The resulting rapid Joule–Thomson expansion produces intense local cooling, typically to about −70 °C , which freezes and destroys the target tissue. In a simplified first-law energy balance (ΔU = Q − W), negligible heat enters during rapid expansion and energy used in expansion is associated with a sharp temperature fall; more precisely, flow through the throttle is an process rather than piston work. This is the direct thermodynamic basis of cryotherapy . Opening a cylinder valve rapidly expands gas into the regulator, so ice can form on cylinder valves and regulators , potentially causing sticking or malfunction. The converse also matters: rapid compression of gas (for example when a cylinder valve is snapped open) generates intense heat, which can ignite oil or grease contaminants — the reason cylinder valves must be opened slowly and kept grease-free second law states heat flows spontaneously hot → cold and entropy of an isolated system always increases. This explains perioperative heat loss to the cold theatre via the four mechanisms of heat transfer: — heat transfer through direct physical contact, e.g. from the patient to a cold operating table; normally a small share (<5%). — heat carried away by the bulk movement of fluids (gases or liquids), e.g. theatre air currents (laminar flow) sweeping warmed air from the skin surface. — heat transfer via infrared electromagnetic waves, which requires no medium, e.g. an exposed patient radiating to cold theatre walls and equipment; usually the largest single mechanism. — heat lost as liquid turns to gas, drawing on the latent heat of vaporisation, from skin, the respiratory tract and open surgical wounds. radiation ≈ 40–60% convection ≈ 30% evaporation up to 20% , with conduction contributing only a small share; an older, widely-quoted breakdown from Sessler (Anesthesiology 2008) gives radiation ≈ 40%, convection ≈ 30%, evaporation ≈ 25% and conduction ≈ 5%. Under general anaesthesia these proportions change significantly as behavioural and autonomic responses are lost: radiation becomes the dominant mechanism, accounting for up to of heat loss, while convective and evaporative losses are comparatively smaller . Both data sets vary considerably with exposed surface area, ambient airflow, surgical irrigation and whether the patient is awake or anaesthetised. The third law Heat to warm 1 L of crystalloid from 20 °C to 37 °C Approximately 71 kJ. Each litre of 20 °C fluid effectively cools the patient by transferring this much heat away from them if not warmed. Spirometry temperature correction (BTPS) ≈4.23 L (an increase of ~5.8%), illustrating why temperatures in gas law calculations must always be converted to Kelvin. All other units are derived from these (e.g. pascal = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², joule = kg·m²·s⁻²). State the first and second laws of thermodynamics with one anaesthetic example. First law — energy is conserved; ΔU = Q − W. Example: heat lost by patient (Q) = heat absorbed by cold IV fluids + heat lost by evaporation from open body cavity. Second law — entropy of an isolated system always increases; heat flows from hot to cold. Example: warming a patient requires an active energy input (forced-air warmer), it does not happen spontaneously. What is the triple point of water and why is it important? The unique temperature and pressure (273.16 K, 611.657 Pa) at which solid, liquid and vapour water coexist in equilibrium. It defines the kelvin scale: 1 K = 1/273.16 of the temperature of the triple point. Used as the primary calibration point for thermometers because it is highly reproducible. (c ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg/K, density ≈ 1 kg/L) Q = m × c × ΔT m = 1 kg, c = 4.18 kJ/kg/K, ΔT = 17 K Q = 1 × 4.18 × 17 = 71.1 kJ This is the basis for fluid warmers — significant energy is needed, hence the need for high-power countercurrent or dry-heat warming devices to keep up at infusion rates >500 ml/min. The SI system provides a coherent framework for all physical measurements in medicine. The gas laws — all derivable from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT — have direct clinical applications from altitude physiology to anaesthetic vaporiser function. Thermodynamics governs heat transfer, phase changes, and energy conservation, with immediate relevance to perioperative temperature management, vaporiser physics, and cryotherapy.

Real gases and the van der Waals equation

Ideal-gas theory makes two assumptions that real gases violate: (1) molecules have negligible volume compared with the container, and (2) there are no intermolecular forces. # Mathematical Concepts Graph shapes, exponentials, logarithms, sigmoid curves and their physiological and pharmacokinetic applications First order Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot. Zero order The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved. Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution Volume of distribution (Vd) is the theoretical volume that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma; a large Vd (e.g. amiodarone, digoxin) implies extensive tissue binding. Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma irreversibly cleared of drug per unit time (e.g. mL/min), reflecting hepatic metabolism and renal excretion. The elimination rate constant links them: k = CL ÷ Vd t½ = 0.693 ÷ k , substitution gives t½ = (0.693 × Vd) ÷ CL . Half-life is therefore directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to clearance: a drug with a large Vd (more reservoir to empty) has a long half-life even with normal clearance, and halving clearance (renal failure) doubles the half-life at constant Vd. This is why changing half-life cannot be predicted from clearance alone sum of exponentials + B·e method of residuals (curve stripping): Plot log concentration against time and fit a straight line to the terminal linear portion (the β/elimination phase). that line back to the y-axis; its intercept is B and its slope is −β/2.303. At each early time point, subtract the extrapolated value from the measured value to give the residual. Plot the residuals on the same semi-log axes: they form a new straight line whose intercept is A and slope −α/2.303 — the distribution phase. Repeat once more if a rapid initial phase remains, as for a three-compartment model (π, α, β). log concentration extrapolated β line residual α line measured curve rate constants α and β (and hence the distribution and terminal half-lives), while the intercepts A and B allow the compartmental micro-rate constants, V₁ and clearance to be derived. This is how the classic propofol and thiopentone kinetic data — a rapid distribution phase followed by slower elimination — were originally characterised, and it explains why a single "half-life" is meaningless for such drugs : as substrate concentration rises, the reaction rate approaches a ceiling. The Michaelis-Menten equation × [C]) ÷ (K + [C]) (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V . K is inversely related to the enzyme's for its substrate: a low K means high affinity (half-maximal rate reached at low concentration). Substrate concentration [C] Vmax (zero-order plateau) First-order: rate ∝ [C] ) the equation simplifies to Rate ≈ (V ) × [C] — rate is proportional to concentration, i.e. first-order kinetics . At high concentrations ([C] ≫ K ) it simplifies to Rate ≈ V zero-order kinetics . The graph therefore transitions smoothly from first-order to zero-order as enzymes saturate. Clinically this is the model for (small dose increments cause disproportionate rises in plasma level near saturation) and (saturated even at social doses, giving a constant elimination of roughly one unit per hour), as well as salicylates and thiopentone in overdose Categorical data are nominal (unordered groups, such as blood group) or ordinal (ordered categories, such as pain score). Numerical data are discrete counts or continuous measurements. The mean uses every value and suits approximately normal continuous data but is sensitive to outliers. The median is the middle ranked value and is preferred for skewed or ordinal data. The mode is the most frequent value and can describe categorical data. Spread and precision Variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean; SD is its square root. Population SD divides squared deviations by N, whereas sample SD divides by n − 1 to reduce bias when estimating the population. The IQR is Q3 − Q1 after ranking observations and spans the middle 50%, so it suits skewed data. SEM = sample SD/√n describes precision of the sample mean, not population variability. normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean = median = mode; approximately 68% of observations lie within 1 SD, 95% within 1.96 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean. Positive skew has a long right tail and usually mean > median; negative skew has a long left tail and usually mean < median. A 95% confidence interval gives a range within which we are 95% confident that the true population parameter lies (strictly, 95% of intervals from repeated samples would contain it); its width communicates precision. For a difference between groups, a 95% CI that excludes zero corresponds to statistical significance at p < 0.05 in a two-sided test. For a ratio, the null value is 1 rather than zero t½ = τ × ln(2) = 0.693 × τ . The empirical Hill equation is fractional occupancy = [A]ⁿ/(K ⁿ + [A]ⁿ), where the Hill coefficient n is an index of cooperativity and curve steepness. When n > 1, binding is positively cooperative: one ligand increases affinity for the next (oxygen binding to haemoglobin; n ≈ 2.7). When n = 1, sites behave independently with no cooperativity (for example myoglobin or a simple drug–receptor interaction). When n < 1, binding is negatively cooperative: one ligand reduces affinity for subsequent ligand. The coefficient is not necessarily the number of binding sites ; it is an empirical summary of interaction. In pharmacology, plotting dose on a logarithmic axis converts the hyperbolic dose-response into its familiar sigmoid shape, with EC₅₀ at the midpoint. The central portion can be linearised using a probit or logit transformation Probit and logit transformations 'stretch' the y-axis of the sigmoid quantal dose-response curve, converting its central portion into a straight line. Linearisation allows simple linear regression ED₅₀ and ED₉₅ are read off accurately and the potency (position) and slope (variability of response) of different drugs compared statistically. Probit analysis assumes an underlying normal distribution of individual effective doses; the logit assumes a logistic distribution and gives almost identical results in practice Pre-oxygenation wash-in time End-tidal O₂ reaches ~95% after roughly one minute (3 time constants). The Association of Anaesthetists recommends pre-oxygenation for at least 3 minutes of tidal breathing, or until end-tidal O₂ exceeds 90% (Recommendations for standards of monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery 2021). The guideline itself is not framed in terms of time constants, but this calculation illustrates the safety margin it provides: 3 minutes extends well beyond the ~1 minute (3τ) needed for 95% wash-in, so the process is effectively complete (>5τ). Why a single time constant fails for remifentanil Equating CSHT to a first-order t½ is a fundamental pharmacokinetic error: remifentanil's offset is multi-exponential and its CSHT (~3–4 min) stays short only because rapid metabolism by non-specific esterases dominates redistribution. Use single-τ models only for genuine single-compartment processes such as nitrogen wash-out or capacitor discharge. Recognising the shape of a graph — linear, exponential, sigmoid, hyperbolic — allows you to predict how a system will behave when variables change. This topic covers the key mathematical relationships encountered in anaesthesia and intensive care, with clinical examples for each.

First order

Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant fraction is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot.

Zero order

The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant amount is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved.

Most drugs follow first-order kinetics at therapeutic concentrations; capacity-limited examples include ethanol, phenytoin at high concentrations and salicylate in overdose Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution

Volume of distribution (Vd) is the theoretical volume that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma; a large Vd (e.g. amiodarone, digoxin) implies extensive tissue binding. Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma irreversibly cleared of drug per unit time (e.g. mL/min), reflecting hepatic metabolism and renal excretion. The elimination rate constant links them: k = CL ÷ Vd.

Since t½ = 0.693 ÷ k, substitution gives t½ = (0.693 × Vd) ÷ CL. Half-life is therefore directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to clearance: a drug with a large Vd (more reservoir to empty) has a long half-life even with normal clearance, and halving clearance (renal failure) doubles the half-life at constant Vd. This is why changing half-life cannot be predicted from clearance alone sum of exponentials:

At depth the ambient pressure is high, so PN₂ is high and proportionally more nitrogen dissolves in blood and tissues — fat and other lipid-rich tissues load slowly but hold most. On rapid ascent the ambient pressure and hence solubility fall faster than nitrogen can be carried to the lungs; the tissues become supersaturated and N₂ leaves solution as bubbles, causing joint and tissue damage ('the bends'), vascular occlusion, and pulmonary or neurological injury. Treatment is recompression with hyperbaric oxygen, which shrinks the bubbles (Boyle's law) and washes out nitrogen down a steep diffusion gradient. Nitrogen narcosis. Clinical Implication
Isolation Transformer & Line Isolation Monitor (LIM)
Group 2 medical locations
, in which the standard earthed mains supply is replaced by an
isolated power system
. A 1:1 isolation transformer magnetically couples power to the theatre but removes the earth reference — both downstream conductors "float" relative to earth. Because no normal return path exists through earth, a patient or staff member touching a single live conductor cannot complete a circuit and no current flows through them.
Line Isolation Monitor (LIM)
continuously measures the impedance from each line to earth. A single insulation fault is detected and alarmed when the fault would permit a
prospective fault current of about 2–5 mA
to flow were a second fault to occur (the exact set point depends on the standard and the device)
, but the supply is deliberately
automatically interrupted — abrupt loss of power to a ventilator or bypass pump may be more dangerous than the fault itself. Two simultaneous faults are required for a hazardous shock.

. An RCD compares the live and neutral currents through a single toroidal current transformer; any imbalance > 30 mA triggers disconnection within 40 ms — fast enough to prevent ventricular fibrillation in most macroshock scenarios. RCD-protected earthed mains is the arrangement used in general clinical areas; in Group 2 locations this auto-disconnect is itself a hazard, so an isolated supply with insulation monitoring is required instead

Diathermy Hazards
Direct coupling
— the activated electrode touches, or arcs to, another conductor in the abdomen (a metal grasper, the laparoscope, a clip). Current passes through that instrument and burns whatever it is holding. Avoid activating while the tip touches other instruments or is outside the field of view.
Capacitative coupling
— an insulated active electrode passing through a metal cannula forms a capacitor (two conductors separated by a dielectric). High-frequency current is induced in the cannula even with intact insulation. If the metal cannula is anchored by a
tissue retainer the induced current has no low-resistance path to the abdominal wall, so it discharges at high current density into adjacent bowel. Use all-metal or all-plastic cannula systems, not hybrid combinations.
Insulation failure
— reusable instruments develop microscopic breaks in the shaft coating from repeated use, cleaning and sterilisation. Current escapes at the defect at high density, typically outside the visual field. Inspect shafts, use single-use or regularly integrity-tested instruments, and remember that higher voltage (coagulation/spray modes) is more likely to breach marginal insulation.
Active electrode monitoring (AEM)
— instruments with a second, earthed conductive shield surrounding the shaft continuously return any stray capacitative or insulation-failure current to the generator, which shuts down if leakage exceeds a threshold; this prevents both mechanisms.
— lowest effective power setting; short, intermittent activations; cut (low-voltage) rather than coag (high-voltage) mode where possible; never activate in open circuit or before the tip contacts the target; keep the whole active tip in view; prefer
or advanced-energy (ultrasonic, vessel-sealing) devices, which confine current between the jaws and avoid a return plate altogether
Theatre Environment — Humidity & Footwear
Why humidity matters
Theatre humidity is maintained at
50–60% relative humidity
(with temperature 20–22 °C).
At low humidity (< 40%), insulating surfaces (vinyl flooring, plastics, drapes, hair, clothing) accumulate
static charge
by triboelectric (friction-induced) charging.
Higher humidity allows a thin film of water on surfaces to act as a
conductive path
, continuously bleeding static charge to earth before it reaches a hazardous potential.
prevents spark formation
— historically critical to avoid ignition of ether/cyclopropane mixtures, but still relevant to: airway fires, alcohol-based skin prep ignition, microelectronic device damage, and patient micro-shock from static discharge to monitoring leads or intracardiac catheters.
Humidity also reduces
skin resistance
in sweating staff and patients — a trade-off that increases macroshock hazard slightly, but the dominant benefit is static dissipation.
Antistatic theatre footwear
Theatre clogs and overshoes are made of
antistatic (conductive) rubber
75 kΩ – 10 MΩ
This range is deliberately chosen as a
"Goldilocks" resistance
Low enough
continuously drain static charge
from the wearer to the conductive theatre floor (and on to earth) — preventing spark discharge.
High enough
limit current flow
if the wearer accidentally becomes part of a mains circuit — at 240 V across > 75 kΩ, current is limited to < 3 mA (well below the 15 mA let-go threshold and the 100 mA VF threshold).
Combined with a
conductive floor
(resistance 20 kΩ – 5 MΩ between two electrodes 60 cm apart), the staff member–shoe–floor system acts as a controlled, slow discharge path.
Pure rubber boots (very high resistance) would
protect against macroshock
but allow
static build-up
— and so are not used in theatre
Diathermy in Patients with Pacemakers and ICDs
Preoperative risk assessment
Identify device
(pacemaker, ICD, CRT, loop recorder), manufacturer, indication and date of last check (within 12 months for a pacemaker, 6 months for an ICD).
pacing dependence
— the underlying rhythm on the device check determines whether loss of pacing is immediately life-threatening.
Discuss with the cardiology or cardiac physiology team; reprogramming (asynchronous pacing, deactivating anti-tachycardia therapies) is required for high-risk surgery, especially above the umbilicus.
Site of surgery matters: monopolar diathermy more than ~15 cm from the device and generator, with a current path away from it, is low risk.
Intraoperative precautions
Bipolar diathermy in preference
— current is confined between the forceps tips, so no current traverses the thorax.
If monopolar is unavoidable: lowest effective power,
short irregular bursts (<5 s)
, cutting rather than coagulation mode where possible, and the return plate positioned so the current path
does not cross
the generator or leads (e.g. thigh for lower-limb or pelvic surgery).
Continuous ECG plus a mechanical means of confirming perfusion (pulse oximetry plethysmograph or invasive arterial trace) — diathermy artefact obscures the ECG.
Immediately available: external defibrillator/pacing pads, a
, chronotropic drugs (atropine, isoprenaline, adrenaline) and the ability to contact the device team.
What does a magnet do?
, a magnet usually switches it to asynchronous (VOO/DOO) pacing at a fixed manufacturer-specific rate, preventing diathermy-induced inhibition — but responses vary and some devices ignore magnets or enter a diagnostic mode. Over an

Magnet response should be confirmed with the device team rather than assumed, and every patient needs a
postoperative device check
before discharge from monitored care.

The capacitor: charge and discharge

E = ½CV²

— current flows in one direction only; historically 200 J escalating to 360 J.
Biphasic truncated exponential (BTE)
— current flows one way then reverses, and the waveform is truncated rather than allowed to decay to zero.
Rectilinear biphasic
— the device actively holds current near-constant during the first phase.
Biphasic devices
measure transthoracic impedance

Transthoracic impedance
Transthoracic impedance (TTI)
is the opposition to current flow through the chest, typically ~70–80 Ω, and determines what fraction of delivered energy reaches the myocardium (I = V/Z). It

Safety during defibrillation
Operator safety: a clear verbal "stand clear" with visual check, oxygen source moved at least 1 m away, no contact with the trolley or wet surfaces, self-adhesive pads in preference to paddles, and charging only once the pads are applied.
Patient safety: correct pad placement (sternal–apical, or anterior–posterior for cardioversion of AF and for patients with a CIED, keeping pads >8 cm from the generator), dry skin, removal of GTN patches, and avoidance of repeated shocks over the same skin to limit burns.
Chest compressions continue while the device charges; the pre-shock pause should be under 5 s.
Paediatric defibrillation
4 J/kg
for paediatric defibrillation. Paediatric attenuator pads or cables reduce the energy delivered by an adult device. If unavailable, use standard adult pads and select the nearest available dose (a 50 J starting setting may be needed on some devices). For infants and children under 10 kg, anterior–posterior placement usually provides enough separation; otherwise use anterolateral placement. Pads must never touch or overlap because this can arc or shunt current away from the myocardium
Synchronised DC cardioversion
a pulse, the shock is
synchronised to the R wave
. Delivering energy during the relative refractory period of repolarisation (on the T wave) can induce VF — the
R-on-T phenomenon
— so the device senses the QRS and times delivery to it. VF and pulseless VT require immediate
defibrillation because there is no organised QRS to synchronise to. Anaesthesia for elective cardioversion aims to provide brief hypnosis and analgesia with minimal cardiovascular depression and rapid recovery — typically a small dose of propofol (or etomidate/ketamine in haemodynamic compromise) with preoxygenation, full monitoring, aspiration precautions and airway rescue equipment, in an area equipped for resuscitation

concentrates current

Apply a full-size plate to shaved, dry, well-perfused muscle bulk close to the operative site, long axis facing the field; never trim it.
Avoid bony prominences, scars, metal implants, ECG electrodes and areas where prep or irrigation can pool.

# Defibrillation & Pacing
Monophasic vs biphasic waveforms, transthoracic impedance, pacemaker modes, and EMI

Monophasic damped sinusoidal (MDS)
waveforms deliver current in a single direction. They require higher energies (up to 360 J for VF) and do not compensate for varying transthoracic impedance. They have been largely superseded by biphasic technology.
Biphasic waveforms
reverse polarity during the shock, delivering current first in one direction then the other. Two subtypes exist:
biphasic truncated exponential (BTE)
rectilinear biphasic (RLB)
. Both achieve equivalent or superior defibrillation success at lower energies (120–200 J), causing less myocardial injury and post-shock ST changes.
impedance compensation
— the waveform automatically adjusts its duration and voltage based on measured transthoracic impedance, ensuring consistent current delivery regardless of patient characteristics.
devices — manufacturer guidance always takes precedence. For monophasic devices, use 200 J for AF and consider 360 J early; double the listed biphasic dose as a rough guide for other rhythms.

Patient and position factors increasing impedance

Technique and equipment factors increasing impedance

reduce impedance

NASPE/BPEG Generic (NBG) code
, a five-position system describing chamber paced (I), chamber sensed (II), response to sensing (III), rate modulation (IV), and multisite pacing (V). Letters used include A (atrium), V (ventricle), D (dual), O (none), I (inhibited), T (triggered), and R (rate-responsive).
(ventricular demand) is the most common single-chamber mode — it paces and senses the ventricle, inhibiting output when intrinsic activity is detected. Its main limitation is
pacemaker syndrome
: ventricular pacing without AV synchrony permits atrial contraction against closed mitral and tricuspid valves, reducing cardiac output and producing fatigue, dizziness, syncope, hypotension and prominent neck pulsations (cannon waves in the JVP). Upgrading to a dual-chamber system restores AV synchrony and usually resolves it.
is the most physiological mode, pacing and sensing both chambers to maintain AV synchrony, and is the mode of choice for complete heart block.
asynchronous mode
(VOO or DOO) — fixed-rate pacing without sensing. This eliminates the risk of EMI-induced inhibition during surgery. The magnet rate also provides manufacturer-specific information about battery status.
Beginning of life (BOL)
describes a fresh battery and its expected magnet rate; at the
elective replacement indicator (ERI)
, the magnet rate is slower and generator replacement should be planned;
end of life (EOL)
denotes advanced depletion and potentially unreliable output or altered device behaviour. A slow magnet rate must be interpreted against the manufacturer chart. ERI/EOL devices need urgent pacing-team review and possible reprogramming or replacement before high-risk surgery, particularly when EMI is expected
include haemodynamically significant symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to drugs, high-grade AV block after myocardial infarction, drug toxicity, and a bridge to recovery or permanent pacing.
Transcutaneous pacing
Apply anterolateral or anteroposterior multifunction pads, select demand mode and a rate around 60–80 min⁻¹, then increase current from about 50 mA until electrical and mechanical capture occurs (often 50–100 mA). Confirm a pulse for every paced complex; provide sedation and analgesia because skeletal-muscle contraction is painful. Limitations are discomfort, artefact and failure to capture.
Transvenous pacing
Insert via the internal jugular or subclavian vein and advance the electrode to the right-ventricular apex under fluoroscopy, intracavitary ECG or pressure-waveform guidance. A typical initial mode is VVI at 70 min⁻¹; set output above the measured capture threshold and sensitivity below the sensed R-wave amplitude. Complications include arrhythmia, failure to sense/capture, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation/tamponade, infection and venous thrombosis.
Transcutaneous pacing is a rapid bridge, not a substitute for prompt definitive planning when ongoing pacing is required
Pacemaker troubleshooting
Failure to capture
A pacing spike is not followed by a P wave or QRS complex. Check cables and lead position; correct ischaemia/electrolytes, increase output (mA), reposition if appropriate and arrange lead review.
Spikes occur despite intrinsic activity. Lead displacement, low-amplitude signals or an insensitive setting may be responsible. Check connections and increase sensitivity by reducing the mV value.
Failure to output
No spike appears despite a rate below the lower limit. Check power, connections and lead integrity; remove EMI causing oversensing and obtain generator support or replacement.
capture: spike → QRS
failure to capture: spike only
undersensing: spike despite QRS

inappropriate tracking

1. Preoperative assessment
Identify the device:
pacemaker, ICD, CRT-P/CRT-D, subcutaneous ICD, leadless pacemaker or implantable loop recorder. Use the patient's device card, chest radiograph and the last interrogation report; note manufacturer, model and implant indication.
within 12 months for a pacemaker and 6 months for an ICD/CRT-D (sooner if symptoms, recent implant <6 weeks, or generator near its elective replacement indicator)
Pacing dependence:
is there an underlying rhythm? Complete AV block, post-AV-node ablation and a persistently paced ECG mean any inhibition may cause asystole.
Programmed settings:
mode, lower rate limit, rate response, magnet response (device-specific — confirm from the manufacturer's chart), and ICD therapy zones.
Functional reserve:
underlying cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction, heart-failure symptoms, valve disease and anticoagulation all shape the anaesthetic technique far more than the device itself.
2. Deciding between magnet and reprogramming
No intervention needed
when EMI risk is low: surgery below the umbilicus with bipolar diathermy or no diathermy, and the patient is not pacing-dependent.
Magnet available and tested
is often enough for short procedures above the umbilicus: over a pacemaker it usually gives asynchronous pacing (DOO/VOO) at a fixed magnet rate; over an ICD it suspends anti-tachycardia therapy but does not change bradycardia pacing.
Formal reprogramming
is preferred when the patient is pacing-dependent and monopolar diathermy will be used above the umbilicus, when the magnet response is unknown/disabled, when the generator is inaccessible under drapes, or for procedures with prolonged EMI (TURP, transthoracic surgery, RF ablation, lithotripsy, MRI, radiotherapy fields).
Rate-response should be switched off
for procedures where ventilation, vibration, shivering or diathermy can be misread as activity (minute-ventilation and vibration sensors are the usual culprits).
3. Intraoperative conduct
External defibrillation/pacing pads applied and connected
any ICD therapy is suspended, positioned anteroposteriorly and at least 8 cm from the generator.
Continuous ECG
a mechanical monitor of perfusion — pulse oximeter plethysmograph or arterial line — because diathermy artefact makes the ECG uninterpretable at the moment risk is highest.
Bipolar diathermy first; if monopolar is unavoidable, use short bursts (<5 s) at the lowest effective power, with the return pad sited so the current vector does not cross the generator or leads.
Immediate access to atropine, adrenaline/isoprenaline, a magnet and an external pacing source; know how to convert to transcutaneous pacing quickly.
Avoid causes of spurious oversensing or arrhythmia: shivering, fasciculations from suxamethonium in a highly sensitive device, central line guidewires displacing recently implanted leads (avoid ipsilateral central access for 6 weeks after implant), and unnecessary hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia.
If the device is a CRT-D, remember that loss of biventricular pacing itself can precipitate decompensation, not merely bradycardia.
4. Recovery and postoperative care
Any suspended ICD therapy must be reactivated before the patient leaves a monitored area — this is a recognised never-event style hazard when handover is rushed. The patient stays on continuous ECG monitoring until therapies are restored.
Re-interrogate after reprogramming, after significant EMI exposure, after external defibrillation/cardioversion, and after any suspected device malfunction; document the restored settings.
Consider extended monitoring or overnight admission where interrogation cannot be completed on the day, particularly in pacing-dependent patients or those with an ICD.

Perioperative Management of Pacemakers & ICDs
What is the difference between monophasic and biphasic defibrillation?
Monophasic — current flows in one direction; 360 J for all shocks (older defibrillators). Biphasic — current reverses direction mid-shock, lowers myocardial damage and skin burns, higher first-shock success at lower energy (120–200 J device-specific). Biphasic is now standard; Resus Council recommends manufacturer
When is synchronised cardioversion indicated and why must the shock be synchronised?
For unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse (AF, atrial flutter, SVT, VT with pulse). Synchronisation delivers the shock on the R wave to avoid the vulnerable T wave period — an unsynchronised shock on the T wave can induce VF. Energy: AF 120–200 J biphasic, atrial flutter and SVT 70–120 J, VT 100 J starting.
What are the indications for temporary transvenous pacing?
Symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine: complete heart block, Mobitz II AV block, alternating bundle branch block, asystole, drug-induced bradycardia (β-blocker, digoxin), peri-procedural for high-risk patients (e.g. RCA PCI with RV infarct). Transcutaneous pacing is the bridge until transvenous access — sedation needed as it is painful.

— fluted profile and larger diameter than the other gas knobs, and colour-coded, so it can be identified by touch alone; one knob per gas, turned anticlockwise to open.
Position of the oxygen flowmeter
— placed downstream of the other gases (right-hand tube in the UK, left-hand in the USA) so that a leak from any other flowmeter tube cannot produce a hypoxic mixture.
Thorpe tube design
— rib guides/ridges centre the rotating bobbin and stop it sticking to the glass, an antistatic coating prevents electrostatic adherence, and an integral stop or cage at the top prevents the bobbin disappearing from view or into the back bar.
Illumination and protective screen
— back-lighting aids reading, and a clear plastic screen in front of the glass tubes protects both tubes and user.
Anti-hypoxia devices

Non-interchangeable, keyed blocks

Bottom line
a fast-moving jet has lower lateral pressure; the Venturi effect uses that to entrain gas through a constriction; the Coandă effect uses the same low-pressure region — this time between the jet and a nearby surface — to bend the jet onto that surface. Constriction flow is symmetric and predictable; jet attachment is asymmetric and surface-dependent.

Recognise the trigger words:

Always state the mechanism:
reduced entrainment between jet and wall → low pressure → jet adheres.
Distinguish from Venturi:
Venturi is constriction-driven entrainment (predictable); Coandă is surface-driven attachment (asymmetric, can flip).
Clinical consequence is what scores marks
— underestimated MR severity, asymmetric ventilation, variable FiO₂ in HFJV, fluidic logic.
Halving ETT diameter — flow consequence
Laminar flow falls 16-fold. Resistance and work of breathing rise dramatically — explaining why even small subglottic oedema in paediatric patients precipitates stridor and respiratory failure, and why suboptimal tube selection is a major contributor to ventilator dyssynchrony.

Heliox reduces gas density and therefore flow resistance under turbulent conditions, raising achievable minute ventilation by ~50% and buying time while definitive airway management is arranged.

What is the difference between laminar and turbulent flow, and which gas laws govern each?
Laminar flow (Re <2000): smooth parallel streamlines, governed by Hagen–Poiseuille — Q ∝ ΔP × r⁴ / (8ηL); depends on viscosity. Turbulent flow (Re >4000): chaotic, Q ∝ √ΔP × r² / √(density × L); depends on density. Reynolds number Re = ρvd/η. In a Venturi or upper-airway obstruction, turbulent flow predominates — hence heliox (low density) helps.
How does a variable-orifice rotameter work?
A vertical tapered tube with a bobbin floating in a gas stream. Flow holds the bobbin at a height where weight = drag force. At low flow, gap is narrow → laminar flow (viscosity-dependent). At high flow, gap is wide → turbulent (density-dependent). Calibration is therefore gas-specific. Bobbin spins to reduce friction; reading is taken at the top of the bobbin.
How does a pneumotachograph measure flow?
Gas passes through a fixed-resistance element (Fleisch — fine-bore tubes; or screen) under laminar flow conditions. The pressure drop across it (measured by differential transducer) is proportional to flow (Hagen–Poiseuille). Integration of flow over time gives volume. Temperature and water vapour must be controlled to maintain calibration.

A child is intubated with a 4.0 mm ID tube instead of an 8.0 mm tube at the same driving pressure. By what factor does laminar flow change, and what is the clinical implication?
Hagen-Poiseuille: Q ∝ r⁴. Ratio = (4/8)⁴ = (½)⁴ = 1/16. Flow through the 4.0 mm tube is 1/16 of an 8.0 mm tube at the same ΔP.
A patient with critical extrathoracic airway narrowing has clearly turbulent breathing. Why does switching from air to a 70:30 helium-oxygen mix improve flow?
In turbulent flow Q ∝ √(ΔP/ρ) — flow depends on density (ρ), not viscosity. Density (g/L): O₂ ≈ 1.43, N₂ ≈ 1.25, He ≈ 0.18. 70:30 He:O₂ density ≈ 0.7 × 0.18 + 0.3 × 1.43 ≈ 0.55 g/L vs air ≈ 1.29 g/L → ~1/2.3 the density. √(2.3) ≈ 1.5 → ~50% increase in turbulent flow at the same driving pressure.

Introduction

Accurate temperature measurement is essential in anaesthesia and critical care. Hypothermia and hyperthermia profoundly affect pharmacokinetics, coagulation, and neurological outcome. Understanding the physics behind different thermometry devices is a core Primary FRCA topic and has direct clinical relevance for choosing the right monitoring site and device.

Interactive Diagrams

Thermocouple — The Seebeck Effect

When two dissimilar metals (e.g., copper and constantan) are joined at a junction, a small voltage (EMF) is generated proportional to the temperature difference between the measuring junction (patient end) and the reference junction. This is the Seebeck effect. Type T (copper-constantan) thermocouples produce approximately 40 μV per °C.

Advantages: Fastest response time (milliseconds), very small probe size, self-generating (no battery), wide temperature range (−200 to +400°C). Disadvantages: Very small EMF requires amplification; needs reference junction compensation (cold junction compensation).

Thermocouple voltage represents T1 − T2, not T1 alone. In modern monitors the reference or “cold” junction is inside the monitor; a thermistor measures that internal temperature (T2), and the electronics add the equivalent reference-junction voltage to calculate patient temperature (T1). This electronic correction replaces the historical ice-bath reference Peltier and Thomson Effects

Peltier effect is the converse of the Seebeck effect: passing a current through a junction of two dissimilar metals causes heat to be absorbed or liberated at that junction, depending on the direction of current flow. It is used for active heating/cooling — thermoelectric coolers, cold-junction compensation, and some blood/fluid warming and targeted temperature management devices Liquid Crystal Thermometers

Disposable forehead strips contain microencapsulated cholesteryl ester liquid crystals. Temperature alters their ordered molecular structure and therefore the wavelength—and colour—of reflected light. They measure skin rather than core temperature, are influenced by ambient conditions and perfusion, and are suitable only for rough trends rather than anaesthetic or critical-care decisions Thermistor — Semiconductor Resistance

A thermistor is a semiconductor (metal oxide bead) with a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) — its resistance falls exponentially as temperature rises. This gives it very high sensitivity (thousands of Ω per °C) but a markedly non-linear response requiring calibration or linearisation circuitry.

Resistance is measured using a Wheatstone bridge circuit. Four resistors — R1, R2, R3 and Rx (the thermistor or RTD) — are arranged in a diamond, with an input voltage Vin applied across one pair of opposite corners and Vout measured across the other pair. The bridge is balanced when R1/R2 = R3/Rx, so Vout is zero; a change in temperature changes Rx, unbalancing the bridge and producing a Vout proportional to the resistance change Vout− Vout+

Wheatstone bridge: balanced (Vout = 0) when R1/R2 = R3/Rx; Rx changing with temperature unbalances the bridge and generates a proportional Vout.

Practical points: a null-deflection version adjusts a variable resistor until Vout is zero (most accurate, no current drawn), while a deflection version reads Vout directly (used for continuous monitoring). A second, identical thermistor in an adjacent arm can compensate for ambient temperature. Long lead resistance introduces error, mitigated by a three- or four-wire RTD connection. Self-heating of the thermistor by the excitation current is itself a source of error, so the excitation current is kept small Resistance Thermometer (RTD/Pt100)

A resistance temperature detector uses a fine platinum wire coil wound around an insulating ceramic or glass core and protected within a probe sheath. Its resistance increases linearly with temperature — a positive temperature coefficient (PTC). The standard Pt100 has a resistance of 100Ω at 0°C, rising by 0.385Ω per °C.

The relationship is described by: Rₜ = R₀(1 + αΔT) where α = 0.00385 Ω/Ω/°C. The linear response is its main advantage over the thermistor. However, it has lower sensitivity and the slowest response time of all electronic thermometers.

Clinical use: its stability, repeatability and near-linear calibration make platinum resistance thermometers laboratory and calibration reference standards. They are rarely used for bedside monitoring because the bridge/readout is relatively complex, lead-wire resistance must be compensated, and the protected coil has low sensitivity, larger thermal mass and a slow response compared with thermistors and thermocouples.

Infrared Tympanic Thermometry

All objects at temperatures above absolute zero emit infrared radiation. The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated is proportional to T⁴ (P = εσAT⁴). An IR tympanic thermometer uses a thermopile (multiple thermocouples in series) to detect the IR radiation emitted by the tympanic membrane.

Although the tympanic membrane is itself supplied predominantly by branches of the external carotid artery, its close anatomical proximity to the internal carotid artery means its emitted infrared radiation acts as a surrogate for the temperature of blood supplying the hypothalamus, making it a reliable reflection of core temperature.

Sources of error: straighten the canal (pinna up and back in adults; down and back in infants), insert far enough to seal it and aim at the tympanic membrane. Cerumen, a narrow or curved canal, otitis externa/media, recent ear surgery, hearing aids, lying on one ear and ambient cold/heat all alter readings. Poor peripheral perfusion in shock can cool the pinna and external canal. Poor alignment samples the cooler canal wall. Devices require regular calibration checks; calibration algorithms differ and population limits of agreement against pulmonary-artery temperature are wide, so a single normal tympanic result must not overrule clinical concern or a reliable central trend.

Clinical Temperature Monitoring Sites

Core sites: PA catheter (gold standard), distal oesophagus (lower third), nasopharynx, tympanic membrane, bladder. Peripheral sites: Axilla, skin (forehead), rectal (delayed response).

Zero-Heat-Flux Thermometry

Principle: a dual-sensor forehead patch (e.g. 3M Bair Hugger temperature monitoring system) contains two thermistors separated by an insulating layer, plus a servo-controlled heating element.

Mechanism: the heater warms the skin until the two thermistors read the same temperature, i.e. there is no temperature gradient and therefore zero heat flux between deep tissue and the skin surface. With heat loss abolished, the skin surface temperature equilibrates with, and so reports, the underlying deep-tissue (core) temperature. Equilibration takes a few minutes after application Fever Monitoring in ICU

# MRI Physics Nuclear spin, precession, T1/T2 relaxation, MRI safety for anaesthetists hydrogen nuclei (¹H protons) , which are abundant in water and fat. Each proton has quantum spin (½) and acts as a tiny magnet. When placed in a strong external magnetic field (B₀), protons align either (low energy, spin-up) or (high energy, spin-down) to B₀. A slight excess align parallel, creating a small but detectable net magnetisation vector (M₀) along B₀. (wobbles like a gyroscope) around the B₀ axis at a frequency given by the Larmor equation: ω₀ = γ × B₀ . For hydrogen, γ = 42.58 MHz/T, giving a Larmor frequency of 63.87 MHz at 1.5T and 127.74 MHz at 3T. An RF pulse at exactly the Larmor frequency transfers energy to the protons (resonance), tipping M₀ away from B₀ into the transverse plane where it can be detected by receiver coils. T1 (spin-lattice/longitudinal) relaxation describes the recovery of magnetisation along B₀ as protons release energy to the surrounding lattice. T1 is the time for 63% recovery. Fat has a short T1 (efficient energy transfer) while water has a long T1 T2 (spin-spin/transverse) relaxation describes the loss of transverse magnetisation as protons lose phase coherence through interactions with neighbouring spins. T2 is the time to 37% remaining signal. 1/T2* = 1/T2 + γΔB₀ . A 180° pulse in a spin-echo sequence rephases the static field component and therefore measures true T2; gradient-echo sequences omit it and retain T2* susceptibility contrast. This makes GRE fast but sensitive to metal, air-tissue interfaces and blood products; susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the effect to demonstrate deoxyhaemoglobin and haemosiderin Image weighting is controlled by TR (repetition time) and TE (echo time). T1-weighted images (short TR, short TE) show fat as bright and water as dark — best for anatomical detail. T2-weighted images (long TR, long TE) show water as bright and fat as dark — best for detecting pathology (oedema, inflammation, CSF). gradient coils explain how signal is localised in three dimensions. Three orthogonal coils (x, y, z) superimpose small, rapidly switched linear variations (a few mT/m) on B₀, so the Larmor frequency becomes a known function of position. Their switching against B₀ generates the Lorentz forces responsible for the characteristic acoustic noise (up to ~110 dB) that mandates hearing protection. Slice selection — a gradient (conventionally z for axial slices) is applied the RF pulse, so only the slab whose precessional frequency matches the pulse's narrow bandwidth resonates. Slice thickness is set by the RF bandwidth and gradient steepness. Frequency encoding — a gradient applied along one in-plane axis during signal readout makes precessional frequency a map of position along that axis. Phase encoding — a brief gradient applied along the remaining axis before readout leaves spins with a position-dependent phase shift . It is stepped through many values (one per line of data), which is why phase encoding dominates acquisition time. , the raw matrix of spatial frequencies: central lines carry contrast and signal-to-noise, peripheral lines carry edge detail and resolution. A two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the final image. Understanding this explains practical anaesthetic points — scan time is driven by phase-encoding steps and repetitions, motion during acquisition corrupts whole k-space lines (ghosting), and even brief patient movement or a laryngospasm episode can force a complete sequence to be repeated Spin echo (SE) A 90° excitation followed by a 180° rephasing pulse corrects static-field dephasing, producing true T2 contrast with fewer susceptibility artefacts, but taking longer. Gradient recalled echo (GRE) Gradient reversal forms the echo without a 180° pulse. It is fast and T2*-weighted, making haemorrhage, haemosiderin, calcification and metal conspicuous. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery is T2-weighted with CSF nulled by an inversion pulse. Periventricular oedema, demyelination and subarachnoid pathology stand out against dark CSF. DWI with ADC Diffusion weighting detects restricted Brownian water motion. Acute cytotoxic oedema is bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map, often within minutes of ischaemic stroke. Susceptibility-weighted imaging combines T2*-weighted magnitude and phase data, making it exquisitely sensitive to paramagnetic blood products. It is used for diffuse axonal injury microbleeds after traumatic brain injury, cerebral cavernomas, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and to distinguish calcification from haemorrhage. four safety zones . Zone I (public), Zone II (screening/questionnaire), Zone III (controlled access, MR-trained personnel only), and Zone IV (the magnet room itself). The 5 Gauss line marks the boundary beyond which the fringe field may affect pacemakers and attract ferromagnetic objects. Missile/projectile effect — ferromagnetic objects (O₂ cylinders, scissors, laryngoscopes, IV poles) are accelerated toward the bore with lethal force; (2) Thermal injury Device malfunction — pacemakers, cochlear implants, and certain aneurysm clips may malfunction, move, or heat. Specific absorption rate (SAR) is RF energy absorbed per unit body mass (W/kg). It rises approximately with B₀² and also with flip angle, RF pulse number/duty cycle and patient size. In normal operating mode, the commonly quoted whole-body limit is 2 W/kg averaged over 6 minutes ; first-level controlled operation permits up to 4 W/kg averaged over 6 minutes under supervision. The scanner estimates SAR and can lengthen TR, reduce slices or reduce flip angle to remain within limits, prolonging the study. Sedated or anaesthetised patients cannot report heating, so remove cable loops, insulate skin-to-skin contact and maintain particular vigilance during long 3 T scans Practical considerations : all equipment must be MR Safe or MR Conditional. Use fibreoptic ECG cables, MR-compatible pulse oximetry, capnography with long sampling lines, and non-ferromagnetic anaesthetic machines and ventilators. Patient access is limited inside the bore — use long breathing circuits and IV extensions. A (rapid boil-off of cryogenic helium) can displace oxygen and cause asphyxiation — emergency ventilation must be available. The 2024 guidance requires a locally rehearsed emergency plan: stop scanning, remove the patient from Zone IV to a predefined resuscitation area, and only then use standard ferromagnetic resuscitation equipment. Screen every person and item before entry, retain equivalent monitoring to the operating theatre, maintain remote visual contact and ensure that airway rescue, fire and quench roles are explicit shortens T1 (and to a lesser extent T2) in tissues where it accumulates, so enhancing lesions appear bright on T1-weighted images. Free Gd³⁺ is toxic, so it is chelated. Chelates are classified by ligand structure (open chain, less stable, more prone to transmetallation and dechelation) versus (a rigid cage that holds the ion far more stably) — and by charge, Group I — high NSF risk Non-ionic linear agents (gadodiamide, gadoversetamide) and ionic linear gadopentetate. Withdrawn or contraindicated in the UK/EU. Group II — low risk Macrocyclic agents: (non-ionic). Standard UK practice; may be used with caution in renal impairment at the lowest diagnostic dose. Group III — intermediate/hepatobiliary Protein-binding linear agents (gadobenate, gadoxetate) with partial biliary excretion, used for liver imaging. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) is a rare, often irreversible fibrosing disorder of skin, joints and viscera occurring weeks to months after exposure. Risk is greatest with linear agents, high or repeated doses and impaired clearance. At-risk groups extend beyond chronic kidney disease with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² to include acute kidney injury (however mild), patients on any form of dialysis, the peri-liver-transplant period , and neonates under 4 weeks whose renal function is immature. Pregnancy exposure should be avoided unless essential . Practical anaesthetic points: check renal function and allergy history before sedating a patient for a contrast study, secure a reliable MR-compatible cannula with an extension so injection can occur from outside the bore, and be ready to manage anaphylaxis in Zone IV — where the patient must first be evacuated to a safe area for resuscitation. Larmor frequency at 1.5 T vs 3 T The RF system must transmit at 64 MHz (1.5 T) or 128 MHz (3 T). The ~4× higher SAR at 3 T means tighter limits on duty cycle, longer scans for SAR-heavy sequences, and a higher index of suspicion for thermal injury — particularly around looped wires, ECG leads and tattoos. Anaesthesia for paediatric brain MRI Use an MR-conditional anaesthetic machine with long circuits, non-ferromagnetic trolley/laryngoscope, fibreoptic monitoring, and check eGFR before gadolinium (selecting a macrocyclic Group II GBCA where renal function is impaired). Maintain access throughout the scan, brief the team on removal to the designated resuscitation area and the quench drill per the Association of Anaesthetists 2024 MRI guideline, and use ear protection for the patient (≥99 dB acoustic noise during scanning). Two distinct mechanisms then generate X-rays:
Bremsstrahlung ('braking radiation')
— the dominant contributor. As an electron is decelerated and deflected by the field of a tungsten nucleus, the lost kinetic energy is emitted as a photon. This produces a
continuous spectrum
from very low energies up to a maximum equal to the tube voltage in keV.
Characteristic radiation
— when an incident electron ejects an inner-shell (K-shell) tungsten electron, an outer electron drops in to fill the vacancy and releases a photon at a discrete energy (~59 and 67 keV for tungsten). This appears as
line peaks
superimposed on the bremsstrahlung continuum.

Four interactions matter clinically; the first two account for almost all relevant medical physics:
Photoelectric effect
— the photon is fully absorbed by an inner-shell electron, which is ejected. Probability is proportional to
— strongly favoured at low energies and high atomic number. This is what gives the bone–soft-tissue contrast on plain films and why iodinated and barium contrast (high Z) work.
Compton scattering
— the photon is partially absorbed by an outer-shell electron and scattered with reduced energy. Dominates above ~100 keV (CT, fluoroscopy primary beam) and is essentially independent of Z. Compton scattering is the source of the
scatter dose
to staff — the patient becomes the principal scatter source inside the room.
Rayleigh (coherent) scattering
— a minor process where the photon is deflected without losing energy. Contributes a small amount to image noise.
Pair production
— a photon (>1.022 MeV) interacts with a nucleus to create an electron–positron pair. Not relevant in diagnostic imaging but matters in radiotherapy and PET.

= table travel per rotation ÷ total beam width along z; pitch > 1 spreads dose over more anatomy (faster, less dose), pitch < 1 oversamples (less noise, higher dose). 64-, 128- and 320-slice detectors allow whole-organ coverage in a single rotation, enabling cardiac and CTPA studies.
Filtered back-projection (FBP)
— the attenuation data from each projection are 'smeared' back across the image matrix. Simple back projection alone gives a blurred image with star artefacts, so the raw data are first passed through a mathematical filter/kernel that sharpens them before back projection — soft-tissue kernels favour low noise, bone/lung kernels favour spatial resolution at the cost of more noise
Iterative reconstruction (IR)
— an initial image estimate is forward-projected to create simulated raw data, compared against the measured data, and the image is repeatedly corrected over successive iterations (e.g. ASIR, IMR, and model-based IR that also models system optics and photon statistics). Lower image noise allows diagnostic images at a significantly lower radiation dose; the trade-offs are increased computation time and an altered, sometimes 'blotchy', image texture

On most modern scanners, however, tube current is modulated in real time to keep image noise constant, so dose does not simply fall as pitch rises

Distinguish three quantities — the exam favourites:
Activity (becquerel, Bq)
— disintegrations per second of a radionuclide source. Not directly relevant to X-ray equipment.
Absorbed dose (gray, Gy)
— energy deposited per unit mass of tissue (J/kg). A purely physical measurement.
Equivalent dose (sievert, Sv)
— absorbed dose ×
radiation weighting factor (wR)
. wR = 1 for X-rays, γ and β; wR = 20 for α-particles. Sieverts therefore reflect biological effect of the radiation type.
Effective dose (sievert, Sv)
— equivalent dose summed across organs, each weighted by a
tissue weighting factor (wT)
that reflects radiosensitivity (e.g. wT = 0.12 for breast, lung, colon, marrow; 0.04 for thyroid; 0.01 for skin). Effective dose is what is reported in personal dosimetry and for comparing risks across imaging modalities.

Stochastic effects
; probability of harm rises with dose, but severity does not. Cancer induction and heritable effects are the principal stochastic risks. Because there is no safe threshold, every avoidable exposure should be avoided.

Doubling the distance cuts dose-rate to ~30 µSv/h (a 4× drop); tripling it to ~13 µSv/h (a 9× drop). Distance is the most powerful single ALARA lever. Combine with a ceiling-suspended lead screen and a 0.5 mm Pb apron and you typically push residual whole-body dose well below 1 µSv/h.

Justify against the clinical question (a missed PE is high-cost), but in a young woman with a normal CXR and clinically suspected PE, V/Q is often the optimised first-line test. Diagnostic X-rays are produced by bombarding a tungsten anode with electrons accelerated across a high-voltage (typically 50–150 kVp) tube — output is a bremsstrahlung continuum plus characteristic K-shell line emissions
kVp controls beam energy (penetration/quality); mAs controls beam quantity (number of photons) — together they determine dose and image contrast
Four photon interactions: photoelectric (∝ Z³/E³, dominant at diagnostic energies, gives bone–soft-tissue contrast), Compton (dominant >100 keV, source of scatter), Rayleigh (minor coherent), pair production (>1.022 MeV only)
Units: activity = becquerel (Bq); absorbed dose = gray (Gy, J/kg); equivalent dose = sievert (Sv) = Gy × wR; effective dose = Sv × tissue weighting factors
ALARA = As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Three pillars: TIME (less exposure), DISTANCE (inverse-square law — doubling distance quarters dose), SHIELDING (0.5 mm Pb apron attenuates ~95% of scatter at 70 kVp)
IRR 2017 occupational limit: 20 mSv/year (avg over 5 years, max 50 mSv/year). Public: 1 mSv/year. Declared-pregnant worker: 1 mSv to the foetus over remainder of pregnancy
Stochastic effects (cancer, hereditary): no threshold, probability rises with dose. Deterministic effects (cataract, skin erythema, marrow suppression): have thresholds — ICRP 2011 lens threshold lowered to 0.5 Gy cumulative
Approximate effective doses: CXR 0.02 mSv · head CT 2 mSv · CTPA 5–10 mSv · abdomen CT 10 mSv · UK background 2.7 mSv/year
Anaesthetist's PPE for fluoroscopy: 0.5 mm Pb wrap-around apron, 0.5 mm thyroid shield, leaded glasses (cataract prevention), and where possible a ceiling-suspended lead screen — plus collar dosimeter outside apron

Step-by-step reasoning
Recognise the pattern: sudden ETCO₂ drop = reduced delivery of CO₂ to alveoli — circulation or circuit problem
Circuit: disconnection, sampling line leak, oesophageal intubation (usually no trace at all), kinked tube — inspect connections and waveform
Circulation: cardiac arrest, massive PE (including CO₂ embolism during laparoscopy), severe hypotension
Suspect CO₂ embolism: stop insufflation, release pneumoperitoneum, place left lateral head-down (Durant), 100% O₂, aspirate via CVC
If cardiac arrest, start ALS; rising ETCO₂ during CPR (>10 mmHg) indicates adequate compressions and possible ROSC
Common traps
Confusing a leak (gradual decline) with embolism (abrupt fall)
Falsely reassuring SpO₂ that lags 20–30 s behind the event
Failing to recognise the diagnostic waveform shapes (curare cleft, obstructive 'shark fin', cardiogenic oscillations)

Modern ventilator drive mechanisms and modes
Pneumatically driven ascending bellows compressed by driving gas in an outer chamber. Fresh gas flow contributes directly to the delivered tidal volume unless decoupled.
Electrically driven linear motor (e.g. Dräger Apollo/Aisys) — quiet, accurate at very low tidal volumes, and enables fresh-gas decoupling; requires a negative-pressure relief/entrainment valve to allow room-air entrainment if the piston outstrips fresh gas supply.

High airway pressure
User-set upper limit exceeded — coughing/straining, kinked tube, bronchospasm, or breath-stacking.
Sustained airway pressure
e.g. >10 cmH₂O sustained for >15 s — suggests expiratory-limb obstruction or a closed/stuck APL valve preventing exhalation.
Low tidal / minute volume
Circuit leak or disconnection, cuff leak, patient effort mismatch, or ventilator fault.
High / low FiO₂
Paramagnetic or galvanic fuel-cell analyser on the inspiratory limb; low-limit typically set 21–25% to detect a hypoxic mixture.
Reverse flow
An incompetent expiratory valve or PEEP valve allows exhaled gas to flow the wrong way, causing rebreathing.
Apnoea alarm
Absent capnography waveform or absent volume signal for a set interval (typically 15–20 s) — capnography is the more sensitive and specific trigger.
alarm fatigue
— repeated nuisance alarms leading staff to widen limits or silence alarms, risking a genuine event being missed
Association of Anaesthetists minimum monitoring standards
Electrical safety
Shock pathways
passes through intact skin; harmful currents are in the milliampere range.
reaches myocardium through an intracardiac conductor, so currents of only tens of microamperes may trigger VF. Keep invasive cardiac conductors isolated and use CF-rated applied parts.
Equipment classes
Class I uses protective earth; Class II uses double/reinforced insulation; Class III is supplied at safety extra-low voltage. Type B applied parts provide basic protection, BF are electrically floating, and CF have the greatest leakage-current protection for direct cardiac application.
Supply protection
Fuses and circuit breakers interrupt overcurrent. Theatre isolated-power systems use an isolation transformer so the first earth fault does not stop supply; a line-isolation monitor alarms falling impedance so the fault can be found before a second fault completes a dangerous circuit.
For monopolar surgery, place the return electrode on clean, dry, well-perfused muscle with full contact and a short current path that avoids metal implants, ECG electrodes and implanted devices. Bipolar current remains between forceps tips and avoids a remote return plate. Inspect insulation and never rely on the return plate as an electrical earth.

Supraglottic airway devices and Aintree catheter
First generation
A single ventilation channel and perilaryngeal seal (classic LMA). Simple rescue oxygenation, but no gastric drainage and less protection from regurgitation.
Second generation
Higher oropharyngeal seal plus gastric drain and often bite block (i-gel, ProSeal, Supreme). Favoured for difficult-airway rescue and selected positive-pressure ventilation.
Intubating devices
Designed as a conduit for tracheal intubation. Some permit fibreoptic-guided passage; blind passage is less reliable and risks trauma.
second-generation SAD
is recommended for rescue oxygenation in difficult intubation
. The
Aintree Intubation Catheter
can be passed over a bronchoscope through a compatible SAD; after SAD removal, a tracheal tube is railroaded over it. Its 15 mm connector allows oxygen insufflation, but only at low pressure with a patent route for expiration
Neuraxial & regional needles
Quincke (cutting)
Sharp medium-bevel — cuts dural fibres → higher PDPH. Standard for diagnostic LP; 25–27G for spinal.
Depth estimation and localisation
Whitacre (pencil-point)
Conical tip with side port — spreads fibres → lower PDPH. Preferred for spinal anaesthesia (25G).
Sprotte (pencil-point)
Longer side aperture → faster CSF flow, more even LA spread.
Tuohy (epidural)
Curved Huber-type tip directs catheter laterally; reduces accidental dural puncture. 16–18G adult.
Huber point (non-coring)
Parts tissue rather than coring — essential for implanted port access.
Stimulating needles
Insulated shaft, exposed tip — short-bevel reduces nerve injury. Often combined with US guidance.

Why vaporisers are FRCA bread-and-butter

Vaporisers convert a liquid volatile agent into a precisely metered vapour added to the fresh-gas flow. The exam tests three things repeatedly: the underlying physics (SVP, latent heat, partial pressure vs percentage), the splitting-ratio calculation, and the engineering of the Tec 6 (the only clinically used vaporiser that is not a variable bypass). Master those and the equipment viva looks after itself.

The Tec 6 — a different beast

  • Sealed reservoir of liquid desflurane heated electrically to 39 °C and pressurised to 2 atm.
  • At 39 °C and 2 atm, vapour pressure of desflurane is ~1.5 atm — always saturated, always above ambient.
  • A microprocessor reads dial position and fresh-gas flow, then opens a flow-control valve to inject measured pure vapour proportionally into the FGF — effectively a gas/vapour blender.
  • Requires mains power and time to warm up (~5–10 min) — clear visual alarms if power fails or warm-up incomplete.
  • Unlike a variable-bypass vaporiser, dialled percentage is held constant even at altitude — but, as with every vaporiser, the partial pressure delivered still falls with Patm.

Mapleson A
(Magill / Lack). During expiration, the first gas expelled (alveolar, high CO₂) leaves through the APL valve sited near the patient. The later expired gas (dead-space, low CO₂) refills the corrugated tubing. Fresh gas entering at the machine end displaces the dead-space gas back toward the patient at the next inspiration — so the patient re-inhales
CO₂-free dead-space gas.

. Mandatory monitors:
