# Neurological Co-Existing Disease
Myasthenia gravis, epilepsy, MS, Parkinson's, MND, muscular dystrophies, spinal cord injury

Step-by-step reasoning
Pre-op: optimise MG (plasma exchange or IVIG if bulbar/respiratory weakness), continue pyridostigmine (omit morning dose to reduce secretions and unpredictable NMJ response), steroid cover
Predict difficult ventilation post-op: vital capacity <2.9 L, disease >6 y, pyridostigmine >750 mg/day, COPD (Leventhal score)
Induction with TIVA (propofol + remifentanil) — avoids volatile-potentiated weakness
Avoid or markedly reduce
non-depolarising NMB
(sensitive — give 10–20% of normal dose, monitor TOF); suxamethonium is resistant (use 1.5–2 mg/kg) but recovery normal
Sugammadex preferred for reversal of rocuronium; plan elective post-op critical care for ventilatory observation
Common traps
Neostigmine reversal can precipitate cholinergic crisis in pyridostigmine-treated patients
Aminoglycosides, magnesium and high-dose steroids worsen weakness
Mistaking myasthenic crisis (weakness improved by edrophonium) for cholinergic crisis (weakness worsened)
Myasthenia Gravis
750 mg/day, VC
Pathophysiology & Assessment
Autoimmune destruction of postjunctional nicotinic ACh receptors → fatigable weakness
Osserman classification: I (ocular), IIA (mild generalised), IIB (moderate), III (acute severe/bulbar), IV (myasthenic crisis)
Associated with thymoma (15%), thymic hyperplasia (65%), and other autoimmune diseases
Predictors of postoperative ventilation: disease duration >6 years, pyridostigmine dose >750 mg/day, VC <2.9 L, bulbar symptoms
Anaesthetic Management
Continue anticholinesterases preoperatively (some omit on morning of surgery to reduce secretions and unpredictable NMBA response)
Non-depolarising NMBAs: exquisitely sensitive — use 10–20% of normal dose (equivalently expressed as 1/10th–1/20th of the ED₉₅); titrate with quantitative neuromuscular monitoring
Suxamethonium: relative resistance (reduced receptors); ED₉₅ is 2.6× normal; phase II block may occur
Sugammadex: preferred for reversal of rocuronium — avoids anticholinesterase interactions
Regional anaesthesia preferred where possible — avoids NMBAs and respiratory depression
Volatile agents provide some muscle relaxation — may allow intubation without NMBAs in mild cases
Postoperative: ICU/HDU for monitoring; plan for possible prolonged ventilation; early extubation with adequate cough, swallow, and VC
Myasthenic vs Cholinergic Crisis
Myasthenic crisis: weakness from disease exacerbation — needs more anticholinesterase or immunotherapy
Cholinergic crisis: weakness from excess anticholinesterase — excessive secretions, bradycardia, miosis
Edrophonium (Tensilon) test can differentiate — improvement = myasthenic; worsening = cholinergic
Quantitative Monitoring, Immunotherapy & Drug Conversion
Quantitative (objective) neuromuscular monitoring — acceleromyography or mechanomyography with TOF ratio — is mandatory throughout, since qualitative/visual TOF assessment cannot reliably detect fade at the safety margins seen in MG; aim for TOF ratio >0.9 before extubation
Sugammadex 2–4 mg/kg reverses rocuronium-induced block reliably even in MG and avoids anticholinesterase-related complications (secretions, bradycardia, unmasking cholinergic crisis); higher doses (up to 16 mg/kg) may be needed for immediate reversal of deep block
Leventhal criteria predict need for postoperative ventilation: disease duration >6 years, coexisting COPD, pyridostigmine dose >750 mg/day, vital capacity <2.9 L — 2 or more positive criteria predicts a high likelihood of requiring postoperative ventilatory support
Pyridostigmine–neostigmine conversion: oral pyridostigmine 60 mg ≈ IV neostigmine 0.5–1 mg (roughly 1/30th the oral pyridostigmine dose) if the enteral route is temporarily unavailable perioperatively; give with glycopyrronium to limit muscarinic side effects
Preoperative optimisation for severe/bulbar/respiratory disease: plasma exchange (typically 5 exchanges over 7–14 days) or IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg) — both produce rapid but temporary improvement (weeks); equivalent efficacy, do not combine
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) — a key exam contrast: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies (often paraneoplastic, small cell lung cancer) cause proximal weakness that
with repeated activity (post-tetanic potentiation), autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth) is prominent, and patients are sensitive to
depolarising and non-depolarising NMBAs — reduce doses of all NMBAs and anticipate a poor/absent response to anticholinesterases
Continue all anticonvulsant medications perioperatively — abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus
Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) → increased hepatic metabolism → faster clearance of opioids, NMBAs, and other anaesthetic drugs
Non-enzyme-inducing: valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine — fewer drug interactions
Valproate: impairs platelet function and coagulation — check FBC and coagulation preoperatively
Drugs that lower seizure threshold (avoid/use with caution): enflurane, tramadol, pethidine, methohexitone, ketamine (controversial)
Safe agents: propofol (anticonvulsant), thiopentone, sevoflurane, isoflurane, fentanyl, rocuronium
Intraoperative seizure management: ensure oxygenation, midazolam 2–5 mg IV, propofol bolus, thiopentone for refractory seizures
Parenteral Equivalents & Perioperative AED Continuity
If the enteral route is unavailable, convert to IV equivalents rather than omitting doses: levetiracetam has 1:1 oral:IV bioavailability (typical 500–1500 mg BD, infused over 15 min); sodium valproate IV is also 1:1 with oral dose; phenytoin can be given IV (loading 15–20 mg/kg, maintenance 100 mg every 6–8 h) with cardiac monitoring (risk of hypotension/arrhythmia with rapid administration, max rate 50 mg/min); carbamazepine has no parenteral formulation — bridge with an alternative (e.g. IV levetiracetam or phenytoin) if NBM for a prolonged period
Missing even a single dose of a long-term AED can precipitate seizures or status epilepticus — liaise with pharmacy/neurology early for complex regimens and prioritise same-day surgery to minimise fasting time
Status Epilepticus: Stepwise Escalation
Definition: a single seizure lasting >5 minutes, or ≥2 seizures within 5 minutes without full recovery of consciousness between them
0–5 min (stabilisation):
ABC, high-flow oxygen, check glucose (give 100 mg IV thiamine + 50 mL 50% glucose if hypoglycaemic or alcohol-dependent), IV access, note time of onset
5–20 min (first-line benzodiazepine):
lorazepam 4 mg IV (repeat once after 10 min if seizure continues) — preferred IV agent; if no IV access, buccal midazolam 10 mg or rectal diazepam 10–20 mg
20–40 min (second-line):
levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g) over 15 min, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV loading (max 2 g, rate ≤50 mg/min with ECG/BP monitoring), OR sodium valproate 40 mg/kg IV (max 3 g) — choice guided by local protocol and comorbidity (avoid valproate in known/possible hepatic disease or childbearing potential)
40–60 min (refractory status — general anaesthesia):
rapid sequence induction with thiopentone 3–5 mg/kg or propofol 2 mg/kg ± infusion, intubate and ventilate, continuous EEG monitoring where available, involve ICU/neurology
Enzyme induction relevance during escalation: patients on enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin) will have accelerated clearance of induction agents, benzodiazepines and NMBAs — anticipate higher maintenance requirements and more rapid emergence from single bolus doses
Multiple Sclerosis
Demyelinating autoimmune disease affecting CNS; relapsing-remitting in 85%
Triggers for relapse: stress, infection, hyperthermia, surgery — avoid perioperative pyrexia
Neuraxial anaesthesia: epidural generally considered safe; spinal anaesthesia more controversial (demyelinated cord exposed to higher LA concentrations)
Use lowest effective concentration of LA for neuraxial techniques
General anaesthesia: all agents considered safe; avoid suxamethonium if significant motor deficit (hyperkalaemia risk from denervation)
Document all pre-existing neurological deficits preoperatively (medicolegal importance)
Disease-modifying therapies (natalizumab, fingolimod): immunosuppressive — infection risk; discuss with neurologist
Relapse Risk, Disease-Modifying Therapy & Spasticity
Perioperative pyrexia (even <1°C rise) can transiently worsen conduction block in demyelinated axons (Uhthoff phenomenon) and is associated with relapse — maintain strict normothermia with active warming and antipyretics for fever
Physiological and psychological stress of surgery/illness is an independent relapse trigger, independent of anaesthetic technique — counsel patients that relapse risk relates more to the surgical stress response and infection than to the anaesthetic agents chosen
Disease-modifying therapies: interferon-beta and glatiramer acetate carry low infection/interaction risk; natalizumab, fingolimod, alemtuzumab and ocrelizumab are more potently immunosuppressive — increased risk of infection (including opportunistic, e.g. PML with natalizumab) and may need surgery timed relative to dosing/lymphocyte recovery in discussion with neurology
Baclofen (oral or intrathecal pump) is first-line for MS spasticity; abrupt withdrawal (pump failure, catheter disconnection, running out of oral drug) causes a life-threatening baclofen withdrawal syndrome — high fever, rebound spasticity/rigidity, pruritus, altered mental status progressing to rhabdomyolysis, multi-organ failure and seizures; treatment is prompt restoration of baclofen (oral or intrathecal), IV benzodiazepines for symptom control, and supportive critical care
Continue baclofen perioperatively wherever possible; if an intrathecal pump is in situ, involve the pain/neurosurgical pump team before surgery near the pump/catheter or before any interruption in delivery
Parkinson's Disease
Dopaminergic neuron degeneration in substantia nigra → tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability
Critical: continue levodopa up to time of surgery and restart ASAP postoperatively (via NG if needed)
Abrupt levodopa withdrawal → NMS-like syndrome (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, autonomic instability)
Absolutely avoid dopamine antagonists: metoclopramide, droperidol, prochlorperazine, haloperidol — use domperidone or ondansetron as antiemetics
Autonomic dysfunction: postural hypotension, gastroparesis (aspiration risk), sialorrhoea, bladder dysfunction
Rigidity may impair chest wall compliance and respiratory function
Regional anaesthesia preferred where feasible — avoids polypharmacy interactions
Propofol may cause dyskinesia in some patients; remifentanil and rocuronium are safe
Advanced Therapies
Deep brain stimulation (DBS):
check device manufacturer, battery status and current settings preoperatively with the neurology/functional neurosurgery team; use bipolar diathermy only, with the return (neutral) pad sited remote from the implanted pulse generator and leads; switch the device off before diathermy or external defibrillation to prevent current induction, tissue heating and hardware damage, then confirm settings on reprogramming; stimulation on/off state affects emergence (rigidity/tremor may return when off) and can produce artefact on EEG-based depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring; MRI is generally contraindicated or requires MR-conditional mode and specialist protocols
Duodopa (levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel):
delivered continuously via a jejunal (PEG-J) tube; protect the PEG-J site and stoma during positioning and surgery, and continue the pump perioperatively wherever feasible; if interrupted (e.g. abdominal surgery, tube displacement), plan an equivalent oral, enteral or transdermal replacement using levodopa-equivalent dosing to avoid acute akinesia and NMS-like withdrawal
Apomorphine infusion:
a potent subcutaneous dopamine agonist used for severe motor fluctuations; causes severe nausea and vomiting — pretreat/cover with domperidone; avoid ondansetron and other 5-HT3 antagonists in combination, as this can precipitate profound, severe hypotension and collapse
Rotigotine transdermal patch:
useful bridging therapy when the patient is nil by mouth or the enteral route is unavailable perioperatively; convert the usual oral dopaminergic regimen using published levodopa-equivalent dose tables
Across all regimens, avoid metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol and droperidol — central D2-antagonism can precipitate severe rigidity and an NMS-like crisis
Timing, Route Conversion & Drugs to Avoid
Schedule surgery first on the list and give the usual levodopa dose with a sip of water no more than 30–60 minutes before induction — even a single missed dose can precipitate acute akinesia (severe rigidity mimicking NMS) within hours
If the oral/enteral route is unavailable postoperatively, give levodopa via NG tube (crushed immediate-release preparations, or use a liquid formulation), or convert temporarily to a rotigotine transdermal patch using published levodopa-equivalent dose (LED) tables — apomorphine subcutaneous infusion or intermittent rescue injections (2–10 mg SC) can also bridge severe motor fluctuations under specialist guidance
Drugs to avoid absolutely: metoclopramide, haloperidol, prochlorperazine and other central dopamine (D2) antagonists — precipitate acute severe rigidity/NMS-like crisis; pethidine is specifically dangerous in patients on MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline) — the combination can cause a serotonergic reaction with hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic instability analogous to serotonin syndrome; avoid pethidine and use alternative opioids
Ondansetron or domperidone are the preferred anti-emetics (domperidone does not cross the blood-brain barrier); avoid cyclizine where possible as its anticholinergic/antidopaminergic profile can worsen confusion and rigidity
Acute akinesia (levodopa withdrawal crisis) presents with severe rigidity, inability to move, dysphagia (aspiration risk), hyperthermia, autonomic instability and rhabdomyolysis — treat as an emergency with urgent restoration of dopaminergic therapy (NG levodopa or apomorphine rescue), IV fluids, and supportive critical care; it is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Motor Neuron Disease
Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons; mean survival 3–5 years from diagnosis
Suxamethonium absolutely contraindicated — risk of lethal hyperkalaemia from denervation supersensitivity
Non-depolarising NMBAs: increased sensitivity — use reduced doses with neuromuscular monitoring
Respiratory: bulbar dysfunction (aspiration risk), restrictive defect, weak cough — may not tolerate supine position
Consider awake fibreoptic intubation if difficult airway anticipated
Discuss advance care planning: DNR status, NIV preferences, feeding decisions
Respiratory Assessment and Ventilatory Support
Symptoms of respiratory muscle weakness: orthopnoea, morning headache (nocturnal hypercapnia), daytime somnolence and fatigue, weak/ineffective cough with poor secretion clearance
Bedside measures: sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (SNIP), supine vs erect FVC (a fall of >20–25% supine indicates diaphragmatic weakness), FVC <50% predicted marks significant respiratory muscle involvement and prompts NIV assessment
NIV (typically bilevel) for nocturnal hypoventilation improves quality of life and survival; initiate for symptomatic nocturnal hypoventilation, orthopnoea, or FVC/SNIP decline even before daytime hypercapnia develops — early initiation is key
Sialorrhoea management: glycopyrronium (reduces secretions with less CNS penetration than hyoscine), hyoscine hydrobromide transdermal patch, atropine eye drops given sublingually, or botulinum toxin injection into salivary glands for refractory cases
Aspiration risk from bulbar weakness drives early consideration of gastrostomy (PEG/RIG) for nutrition — ideally performed before FVC falls below ~50% predicted, as respiratory reserve dictates procedural risk and anaesthetic technique
Anaesthetic Care and Advance Care Planning
Suxamethonium absolutely avoided — denervation-related upregulation of extra-junctional receptors risks life-threatening hyperkalaemia
Marked sensitivity to non-depolarising NMBAs — use reduced doses with mandatory quantitative (TOF) monitoring; sugammadex reversal for rocuronium
Increased sensitivity to opioids and sedatives — titrate cautiously, favour short-acting agents, and anticipate exaggerated respiratory depression
Use regional or local anaesthetic techniques wherever feasible to avoid airway instrumentation and systemic sedation
High risk of postoperative ventilator dependence in patients with pre-existing respiratory muscle weakness — plan critical care disposition and discuss realistic weaning/extubation goals before surgery
Early and ongoing advance care planning is essential: agree a ceiling of treatment and complete a ReSPECT (or equivalent) form; discuss tracheostomy ventilation as a treatment option and the patient's wishes regarding it; where ventilatory support is to be withdrawn, plan this with anticipatory symptom control (opioids, benzodiazepines) and specialist palliative care input
Muscular Dystrophies
Duchenne MD: X-linked recessive; cardiomyopathy develops by teens; scoliosis → restrictive lung disease
Suxamethonium contraindicated in ALL muscular dystrophies — risk of rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, and cardiac arrest
Volatile agents: risk of rhabdomyolysis/MH-like reaction (not true MH but clinically similar) — TIVA recommended
Cardiomyopathy: preoperative echocardiography essential; avoid myocardial depressants
Myotonic dystrophy (DM1): myotonia (sustained contraction not reversed by NMBAs), cardiomyopathy, conduction abnormalities (require preop ECG), central and obstructive sleep apnoea
Myotonia triggers: suxamethonium, neostigmine, hypothermia, shivering, diathermy
TIVA with propofol/remifentanil is preferred; use sugammadex for reversal if rocuronium used
Myotonic Response, Rhabdomyolysis & MH Relationship
Myotonia is a failure of muscle relaxation after voluntary contraction or stimulation due to abnormal sarcolemmal chloride/sodium channel function — it is
abolished by non-depolarising NMBAs or regional anaesthesia because the defect is in the muscle membrane itself, distal to the neuromuscular junction
Recognised precipitants of myotonic contracture: cold (theatre hypothermia), shivering, mechanical/electrical stimulation (diathermy, surgical handling), and neostigmine (anticholinesterase reversal can provoke severe generalised myotonia) — maintain strict normothermia with forced-air warming and avoid neostigmine where possible, preferring sugammadex for rocuronium reversal
Suxamethonium is contraindicated in all dystrophies/myotonic disorders — triggers sustained myotonic contracture that can make bag-mask ventilation and intubation impossible, in addition to the risk of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest
Volatile-agent exposure in Duchenne/Becker dystrophinopathies can trigger an MH-like reaction (acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia, hyperthermia and cardiac arrest) that is clinically similar to but pathophysiologically distinct from true malignant hyperthermia (dystrophin deficiency rather than ryanodine receptor mutation); dantrolene is still used in treatment of this reaction, and TIVA is preferred to avoid it entirely

Perioperative anaemia (incl. iron deficiency), thrombocytopenia and neutropenia — patient blood management, transfusion thresholds and procedural safety

Step-by-step reasoning

Investigate the cause (GI source mandatory in this age group — already being addressed by the surgical pathway).
Surgery is <6 weeks away → IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg or ferric derisomaltose up to 20 mg/kg) is preferred over oral iron (NATA 2017; CPOC 2023). Allow ≥2 weeks for Hb response.

Common traps
Giving oral iron when surgery is <6 weeks — too slow.

Anaemia & Iron Deficiency
Definition & Why It Matters
WHO: Hb <130 g/L (men), <120 g/L (non-pregnant women), <110 g/L (pregnancy)
Present in 30–40% of patients listed for major surgery; independently associated with mortality, allogeneic transfusion, AKI, infection and length of stay
Iron deficiency (absolute or functional) is the commonest cause and is treatable
Elective Pathway (CPOC 2023 / NATA 2017)
Screen at the point of listing — allow ≥6 weeks before surgery for investigation and treatment
Minimum panel: FBC, ferritin, TSAT, B12/folate, U&Es, CRP (functional iron deficiency = ferritin <100 µg/L or TSAT <20% with inflammation)
Iron deficiency: oral iron (ferrous sulphate 200 mg od/alt-day) first-line if surgery is >6 weeks away; otherwise
IV iron
— single dose, response in 1–2 weeks, so give ≥2 weeks before surgery
Treat B12/folate deficiency, refer for GI evaluation in unexplained IDA
Consider erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in selected renal/chemotherapy-related anaemia (specialist input)
transfuse to "top up" preoperatively — outcomes are worse than treating the underlying cause
IV Iron: Choice, Risks & Contraindications (MHRA 2013)
Ferric carboxymaltose:
up to 1000 mg per dose (max ~20 mg/kg), infused over ≥15 minutes; can usually be given as a single dose
Ferric derisomaltose (iron isomaltoside):
up to 20 mg/kg as a single dose, infused over ~20–30 minutes regardless of dose size
all IV iron carries a small but real risk — give only where staff are trained to recognise and treat anaphylaxis, resuscitation facilities are immediately available, and the patient is observed for at least 30 minutes after completion of the infusion (MHRA 2013)
Fishbane reaction:
a non-allergic, self-limiting flushing/chest-tightness/back-pain reaction — slow or pause the infusion; does not require adrenaline or discontinuation of future IV iron
more common and potentially more prolonged/symptomatic with ferric carboxymaltose (FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting) — check phosphate if bone pain, myalgia or fatigue develop post-infusion, particularly with repeated dosing
known hypersensitivity to the product, anaemia not due to iron deficiency, evidence of iron overload or disturbances of iron utilisation, active infection/sepsis (may fuel bacterial growth), first trimester of pregnancy
Expect a haemoglobin response within 1–2 weeks — give IV iron at least 2 weeks before surgery wherever the pathway allows
Urgent / Emergency Surgery
Do not delay life- or limb-saving surgery for elective optimisation
Activate major haemorrhage protocol early; aim Hb ≥70 g/L (≥80 g/L with ACS / chronic cardiovascular disease) — NICE NG24
Use a 1:1:1 ratio of red cells:FFP:platelets in massive transfusion; add cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (<2 g/L in obstetrics)
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction and 1 g at the end of surgery (POISE-3, 2022); within 3 hours of trauma (CRASH-2) or postpartum haemorrhage (WOMAN)
Use intra-operative cell salvage where feasible (including obstetrics and cancer surgery with leucodepletion filter)

Seizure risk:
TXA is a competitive antagonist at glycine and GABA-A receptors; risk rises with high dose, cardiac surgery (especially open-chamber/on-pump procedures) and renal impairment where clearance is reduced — dose-reduce in renal failure. New myoclonus or seizure requires drug review and supportive management (
Thrombotic risk:
POISE-3 showed less bleeding with TXA but did not establish non-inferiority for the composite cardiovascular outcome, so a documented risk/benefit judgement is still needed in patients with a recent thrombotic event (

Wrong-route error:
inadvertent intrathecal administration (ampoule confusion with bupivacaine) causes refractory seizures, ventricular arrhythmia and high mortality — store TXA separately from local anaesthetics, label ampoules/syringes distinctly, and perform a read-back check of the drug name before any neuraxial injection.
Intra-operative Patient Blood Management
Maintain normothermia, normocalcaemia and pH >7.2 — all support haemostasis
Avoid hypotensive episodes that drive ischaemia in anaemic patients
Use viscoelastic testing (ROTEM/TEG) to guide component therapy in major bleeding
Minimise iatrogenic blood loss (microsampling tubes, judicious phlebotomy)
Identify the cause before transfusing: drug-induced (heparin → HIT, alcohol, chemotherapy), liver disease/hypersplenism, ITP, TTP/HUS, DIC, gestational thrombocytopenia, dilutional
Check trend, MCV, blood film, coagulation screen, fibrinogen, LDH, haptoglobin and renal function
Examine for petechiae, mucosal bleeding and splenomegaly
Differentiating Thrombotic Microangiopathies (TTP vs HUS)
Both present with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, negative DAT) and thrombocytopenia with a normal coagulation screen — but management diverges sharply, so the distinction is urgent.
: fluctuating neurological signs (confusion, focal deficits, seizures), fever, profound thrombocytopenia (often <30 ×10⁹/L) with only modest renal impairment; caused by deficiency of ADAMTS13 (usually acquired autoantibody) leaving ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to drive platelet microthrombi
Typical (STEC) HUS

Atypical HUS
: complement dysregulation, no diarrhoeal prodrome, often relapsing with severe renal failure and a family history
Key investigations

plasma exchange), ADAMTS13 inhibitor/antibody, stool Shiga toxin PCR, complement C3/C4 and functional complement studies, pregnancy test, HIV, and a coagulation screen to exclude DIC
PLASMIC score
(Platelets <30 ×10⁹/L; haemolysis; no active cancer; no transplant; MCV <90 fL; INR <1.5; creatinine <177 µmol/L) — a score of 6–7 indicates high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency and justifies starting plasma exchange before the assay returns
Immediate management

Typical HUS — supportive care with fluids and renal replacement therapy as needed (avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents). Atypical HUS — complement inhibition with eculizumab.

Procedural Platelet Thresholds (BSH 2017 / AAGBI 2013)
≥20–30 ×10⁹/L: low bleeding-risk procedures (central line, paracentesis)
≥50 ×10⁹/L: most major surgery and lumbar puncture
≥80 ×10⁹/L: neuraxial (spinal/epidural) anaesthesia, including epidural catheter removal
≥100 ×10⁹/L: neurosurgery, posterior-eye surgery, cardiopulmonary bypass
For obstetric epidurals, count must be stable and trending upwards if low; obstetric haematology input if <80 ×10⁹/L
Anaesthetic Implications
Prefer general over regional anaesthesia where count is below threshold or trajectory unclear
Avoid IM injections, nasogastric tube force, and unnecessary arterial/CVC lines; ultrasound for all vascular access
Use TXA, careful surgical haemostasis and intra-operative monitoring of platelet count in prolonged surgery
Do not transfuse platelets in HIT, TTP, or chronic ITP without haematology advice

HIT: stop all heparin (including line flushes), switch to argatroban or fondaparinux, send HIT antibody screen
Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
IgG antibodies form against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes; immune complexes cross-link and activate platelets via the FcγRIIa receptor, triggering thrombin generation and a paradoxically
state despite a falling platelet count (ASH 2018)
4Ts pre-test probability score
— Thrombocytopenia (magnitude/pattern of fall), Timing (onset 5–10 days after heparin exposure, or <24 h with recent heparin exposure in past 100 days), Thrombosis (new venous/arterial event, skin necrosis, or acute systemic reaction), oTher causes excluded: score 0–3 low probability (HIT essentially excluded, do not test), 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high probability (send immunoassay and consider empirical non-heparin anticoagulation while awaiting results)
PF4–heparin immunoassay (ELISA) is sensitive but poorly specific (many false positives, especially post-cardiac surgery); confirm a positive or intermediate/high 4Ts result with a functional assay — serotonin release assay (SRA) or heparin-induced platelet activation assay (HIPA)
Immediate management:
heparin exposure — unfractionated heparin, LMWH, heparin flushes and heparin-bonded catheters — and start therapeutic-dose non-heparin anticoagulation even in the absence of confirmed thrombosis (subclinical/occult thrombosis is common)
Non-heparin anticoagulants:
argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, hepatically cleared — preferred in renal failure; start ~0.5–2 microgram/kg/min, lower end in critical illness or hepatic dysfunction, titrate to APTT 1.5–3.0× baseline; falsely prolongs INR, complicating warfarin transition); bivalirudin; fondaparinux (weight-banded 5 mg <50 kg / 7.5 mg 50–100 kg / 10 mg >100 kg subcutaneously once daily — avoid in significant renal impairment); DOACs once platelets have recovered
Platelet transfusion:
avoid unless active, significant bleeding — transfusion may fuel the prothrombotic process and precipitate arterial or venous thrombosis
defer until platelets have recovered to >150 ×10⁹/L, and overlap with a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant for at least 5 days — starting warfarin early risks venous limb gangrene from unopposed protein C/S depletion
Duration of anticoagulation:
at least 4 weeks if no thrombosis identified; at least 3 months if HIT-associated thrombosis has occurred
Document a clear heparin allergy/alert on the drug chart and discharge summary — re-exposure risk persists for years
Emergency Surgery with Severe Thrombocytopenia
Discuss with haematology; consider IV immunoglobulin and steroids in ITP, plasma exchange in TTP
For active bleeding, target platelet count >50 ×10⁹/L (or >100 ×10⁹/L for CNS/eye surgery)
Correct associated coagulopathy: fibrinogen >1.5 g/L, INR <1.5, normothermia, ionised Ca²⁺ >1.1 mmol/L
Consider DDAVP 0.3 µg/kg in uraemia or aspirin-induced platelet dysfunction
For the bleeding patient tonight:
platelet-sparing second-line ITP agents (below) are
fast-acting enough — mainstays remain IVIg 1 g/kg (onset 24–48 h), high-dose corticosteroids, and platelet transfusion given
rather than before surgery to avoid consumption by circulating antiplatelet antibodies
Second-line agents for chronic ITP (planned/semi-elective surgery only):
thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor agonists — eltrombopag (oral, 25–75 mg daily, taken away from food and calcium-containing products, requires hepatotoxicity monitoring) and romiplostim (weekly subcutaneous injection, 1–10 mcg/kg) — stimulate megakaryopoiesis to raise the platelet count and avoid the alloimmunisation and refractoriness risks of repeated platelet transfusion; other second-line options include rituximab, splenectomy, and fostamatinib where available
TPO agonists have a typical onset of 1–2 weeks with peak effect at 2–4 weeks, so they are only suitable when surgery can be planned or is semi-elective/urgent rather than immediate; specialist haematology input is required, TPO agonists carry a thrombotic risk if the platelet count overshoots, and dosing should be timed so the count peaks on the day of surgery
Von Willebrand Disease
Definition & Epidemiology
Deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (VWF), a large multimeric glycoprotein that mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen at sites of vascular injury and carries and stabilises factor VIII, protecting it from proteolysis in plasma
The most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting up to 1% of the population, though only around 0.01% are clinically symptomatic; usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Classification & Treatment Implications
Type 1
(70–80% of cases): partial quantitative deficiency of VWF; usually mild and DDAVP-responsive
Type 2
(subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N): qualitative defects in VWF function; DDAVP is generally ineffective and is relatively contraindicated in type 2B, where it can worsen thrombocytopenia by releasing dysfunctional high-molecular-weight multimers that bind platelets and are cleared
Type 3
: near-complete absence of VWF; severe bleeding phenotype requiring factor concentrate rather than DDAVP
Mucocutaneous bleeding, menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising, and post-operative or post-partum haemorrhage
A normal APTT does
exclude von Willebrand disease
Anaesthetic Management
Early pre-operative haematology consultation with subtype confirmation and, where relevant, a documented prior DDAVP trial response
DDAVP (desmopressin):
0.3 mcg/kg IV over 30 minutes, given about 30–60 minutes before surgery, for DDAVP-responsive type 1 disease; tachyphylaxis occurs after repeated doses, and hyponatraemia is a risk — restrict free water, avoid in the elderly and in cardiac disease, and use with caution in children under 2 years
Factor replacement:
VWF-containing factor VIII concentrate (e.g. Haemate P/Voncento) or recombinant VWF for type 2, type 3, or major surgery, dosed in VWF:RCo units to target levels of about 100 IU/dL for major surgery and 50 IU/dL for minor surgery, maintained for several days post-operatively
Tranexamic acid
1 g IV 8-hourly (or oral/topical) as an adjunct, particularly valuable for mucosal surgery
Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, and intramuscular injections
Neuraxial and deep blocks only after correction of the defect and discussion with haematology
Monitor VWF and factor VIII levels post-operatively — the physiological peripartum rise in VWF falls rapidly after delivery, risking delayed post-partum haemorrhage
Definitions & Causes
Mild 1.0–1.5 ×10⁹/L; moderate 0.5–1.0 ×10⁹/L; severe <0.5 ×10⁹/L; profound <0.1 ×10⁹/L
Commonest causes: cytotoxic chemotherapy, haematological malignancy, sepsis, drug-induced (clozapine, carbimazole, sulphasalazine), autoimmune, B12/folate deficiency, congenital
Elective Surgery Planning
Time elective surgery to neutrophil recovery (typically >1.0 ×10⁹/L) when feasible
Discuss with oncology/haematology — chemotherapy timing, G-CSF (filgrastim) prophylaxis, antimicrobial cover
Cancel non-urgent surgery in active neutropenia unless oncologically essential
Perioperative Conduct
Strict aseptic technique for all invasive procedures; ultrasound-guided vascular access; full barrier precautions for central lines and neuraxial blocks
Reverse-barrier nursing where unit policy applies; minimise visitors, avoid rectal temperature probes and per-rectum drugs
Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis per local policy; treat any breach of mucocutaneous integrity aggressively
Recognise blunted inflammatory response — sepsis may present only as fever, hypotension or new organ dysfunction
Neutropenic Sepsis — Emergency (NICE NG141)
Definition: neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L (or expected to fall) with temperature >38°C
other signs of clinically significant sepsis
Within 1 hour:
blood cultures (peripheral and from each lumen of any indwelling line), then empirical IV piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g (or meropenem 1 g if previous resistance/severe penicillin allergy)
Resuscitate per Sepsis-6: O₂, IV fluids, lactate, urine output, source control
Add vancomycin/teicoplanin only for suspected line infection, MRSA risk or severe mucositis
Escalate to critical care early; admit even if initially stable for IV antibiotics and monitoring

Neutropenic patient who is unwell

Peripheral blood cultures
separate cultures from
each lumen

piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV (NICE NG141)

postpone until neutrophils >1.0 ×10⁹/L and afebrile ≥48 h

proceed with antibiotic cover, full barrier precautions, senior anaesthetist + surgeon, HDU/ICU bed booked
do not delay life-saving surgery — give first dose of empirical antibiotics in the anaesthetic room if not already started, take cultures intra-op, plan post-op critical care
Notify haematology/oncology of all neutropenic patients undergoing surgery; consider G-CSF post-op per local protocol

supplemental O₂ throughout (aim SpO₂ ≥95–98%), active warming and warmed fluids, avoid tourniquets where possible (see debate below), maintain euvolaemia with generous IV fluids, avoid prolonged fasting, avoid vasoconstrictors/positioning that impair venous return, treat pain and anxiety early, avoid acidosis (adequate ventilation, avoid hypercapnia)
Preoperative transfusion:
for major/intermediate-risk surgery, a simple top-up transfusion targeting Hb ~100 g/L is as effective as aggressive exchange transfusion at preventing perioperative sickle complications (TAPS trial) and is preferred for most surgery; exchange transfusion (manual or automated) to reduce HbS% to <30% (some centres <20–30%) is reserved for high-risk surgery (cardiopulmonary bypass, neurosurgery, prior severe crises) or when Hb is already high (avoid hyperviscosity from simple transfusion)
Acute chest syndrome:
new pulmonary infiltrate plus one of fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, or hypoxia — treat with high-flow O₂, incentive spirometry, empirical antibiotics (cover atypicals), analgesia titrated to avoid respiratory depression, exchange transfusion for hypoxia or rapid deterioration, escalate to critical care early; a leading cause of death in SCD
Vaso-occlusive crisis:
aggressive IV fluids, high-flow O₂ if hypoxic, early strong opioid analgesia (avoid pethidine — accumulation risk of norpethidine seizures), warmth, treat any precipitant (infection, dehydration, cold exposure)
Tourniquet debate:
tourniquets induce local hypoxia, acidosis and stasis distal to the cuff and are traditionally avoided in SCD; however case series and some genotypes (particularly HbSC) tolerate tourniquets with adequate limb exsanguination, optimisation of HbS% and minimising inflation time — decision should be individualised with haematology input, and tourniquets are generally avoided unless essential for the surgical field
Regional anaesthesia is not contraindicated and may reduce stress-related sickling; avoid excessive vasoconstrictor-containing local anaesthetic solutions and maintain warmth of the limb
HbSC and HbS-β-thalassaemia genotypes are milder than HbSS but still require the same precautions
β-thalassaemia major:
transfusion-dependent from infancy, resulting in chronic iron overload despite iron chelation (desferrioxamine, deferiprone, deferasirox)
Cardiac disease:
iron deposition causes dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias and pulmonary hypertension — the leading cause of death; obtain ECG, echocardiography (and cardiac MRI T2* if available) preoperatively in any transfusion-dependent patient
iron deposition in pituitary, pancreas and thyroid causes diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism and growth/pubertal delay — check glucose and endocrine function preoperatively
Difficult airway:
extramedullary haematopoiesis causes maxillary and frontal bone overgrowth ("chipmunk facies"), maxillary protrusion and dental malocclusion — anticipate a difficult laryngoscopy/mask fit and have airway adjuncts and videolaryngoscopy available

Continue iron chelation; check ferritin and organ function; transfuse to pre-op Hb targets set by the patient's haematologist (typically maintaining pre-transfusion Hb >90–100 g/L in transfusion-dependent disease)

# Hepatic Co-Existing Disease
Cirrhosis, portal hypertension, Child-Pugh & MELD risk, altered pharmacology, coagulation, hepatorenal syndrome, anaesthesia for non-hepatic surgery in liver disease

Step-by-step reasoning
Common traps
Reflexive FFP/platelets to "correct" the INR — increases volume and portal pressure without reducing bleeding.
Withholding VTE prophylaxis because of cirrhosis — VTE risk is preserved; bleeding risk is over-estimated by INR.
Standard paracetamol dosing (4 g/24 h) — reduce to ≤ 2–3 g/24 h in established cirrhosis.
NSAIDs — precipitate AKI/HRS and variceal bleeding; contraindicated.
= [ ["How is preoperative risk stratified in cirrhosis for non-hepatic surgery?", "Combine Child-Pugh class (A/B/C) and MELD score — MELD
Preoperative Risk Stratification
Child-Pugh Score
Five components (1–3 points each):
bilirubin, albumin, INR (or PT), ascites, encephalopathy
Class A (5–6) — well-compensated; B (7–9) — significant functional compromise; C (10–15) — decompensated.
Approximate 30-day perioperative mortality for major abdominal surgery: A ~10%, B ~30%, C > 70%
Limitations: subjective scoring of ascites and encephalopathy; no renal component.
MELD and MELD-Na
Continuous score from
bilirubin, INR and creatinine
(MELD-Na adds sodium).
Better predictor than Child-Pugh for 30- and 90-day mortality after non-transplant surgery — every 1-point rise in MELD above 8 increases mortality by ~1% per point up to MELD 20, then ~2% per point thereafter
Practical thresholds: MELD < 10 → proceed; 10–15 → proceed with caution and optimisation; > 15 → defer or reconsider elective surgery; > 20 → only life-saving surgery, ideally at a transplant centre.
Multidisciplinary Workup
Hepatology review: stage portal hypertension (transient elastography, varices on OGD), exclude HCC, optimise diuretics and beta-blockers.
Cardiac assessment: cirrhotic cardiomyopathy is common — TTE for systolic/diastolic function and pulmonary pressures; CPET helps quantify reserve before major surgery
Anaesthetic plan documented with senior input; consider regional or hybrid techniques and HDU/ICU bed availability.
Systemic Features of Cirrhosis
Cardiovascular — Hyperdynamic Circulation
↑Cardiac output, ↓SVR, blunted response to catecholamines (down-regulated β-receptors).
Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy: latent systolic and diastolic dysfunction unmasked by stress; prolonged QTc in ~50%.
Portal hypertension & aortocaval compression by ascites — preload-dependent state vulnerable to neuraxial blockade and IPPV.
Hepatopulmonary syndrome
: intrapulmonary vascular dilatation → platypnoea, orthodeoxia, A–a gradient > 15 mmHg; supplemental O₂ may be inadequate.
Portopulmonary hypertension
: mean PAP > 25 mmHg with PVR > 240 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵; severe PoPH (mPAP > 45) is a contraindication to liver transplant and a major intraoperative risk.
Ascites and pleural effusion ↓ FRC, predispose to atelectasis and rapid desaturation.
Renal — Hepatorenal Syndrome
Splanchnic vasodilatation → effective hypovolaemia → renal vasoconstriction; functional AKI without structural change.
: HRS-AKI now replaces the old "type 1" HRS, and HRS-NAKI (non-AKI, comprising HRS-AKD and HRS-CKD) replaces "type 2"
Diagnostic criteria
(ICA 2015 / EASL 2018) — all must be present: (1) cirrhosis with ascites; (2) AKI by KDIGO/ICA criteria (creatinine rise ≥ 26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥ 50% above baseline within 7 days); (3) no sustained improvement after ≥ 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and volume expansion with 20% albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day); (4) absence of shock; (5) no current/recent nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast); (6) no macroscopic structural kidney injury — proteinuria < 500 mg/day, no microhaematuria (< 50 RBC/HPF), normal renal ultrasound
: extreme splanchnic arterial vasodilatation from portal hypertension and nitric oxide release reduces effective arterial blood volume, triggering baroreceptor-mediated activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system and vasopressin release, causing intense renal cortical vasoconstriction; cirrhotic cardiomyopathy limits the compensatory rise in cardiac output; systemic inflammation and bacterial translocation contribute.
terlipressin 1 mg IV 4–6 hourly
(or 2 mg/day by continuous infusion), increased to 2 mg 4–6 hourly if creatinine has not fallen by ≥ 25% after 2 days, together with
20% human albumin
(1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/day), continued for up to 14 days or until full response (creatinine within 26.5 µmol/L of baseline);
noradrenaline 0.5–3 mg/h
is an acceptable ICU alternative, titrated to a MAP rise of 10–15 mmHg or MAP > 80–85 mmHg
: hourly urine output, daily creatinine and sodium, fluid balance and body weight (albumin-related overload); watch for terlipressin ischaemic complications (digital, mesenteric, myocardial), hyponatraemia and pulmonary oedema — stop terlipressin if these occur.
Role of RRT
: a bridge to liver transplantation or to recovery from a reversible precipitant, not a treatment for HRS itself; liver transplantation is the only definitive therapy, with simultaneous liver-kidney transplant considered after prolonged dialysis dependence.
Haematological — Rebalanced Haemostasis
Parallel reduction in pro- and anticoagulant factors; thrombocytopenia balanced by ↑vWF; fibrinolysis variable.
INR does not predict bleeding
in cirrhosis — do not transfuse FFP prophylactically
Use TEG/ROTEM where available: target fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L (FIBTEM A10 > 8 mm), treat hyperfibrinolysis with TXA, platelets only if < 50 × 10⁹/L with active bleeding or planned neuraxial.
VTE prophylaxis must not be omitted — risk of portal vein and deep vein thrombosis is preserved or increased.
Neurological — Hepatic Encephalopathy
West Haven grades I–IV; precipitated by sepsis, GI bleed, sedatives, electrolyte derangement, constipation, TIPSS, dehydration.
Mechanism: ammonia, neuro-inflammation, GABA-ergic tone — explains exaggerated sensitivity to benzodiazepines and opioids.
Treatment: lactulose 30 mL 2-hourly until 2–3 soft stools/day, rifaximin 550 mg BD for recurrence prophylaxis
Gastrointestinal & Nutritional
Varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy — anticipate GI bleeding; secondary prophylaxis with non-selective β-blocker or band ligation.
Sarcopenia and protein-calorie malnutrition are independent predictors of perioperative mortality — preoperative nutritional optimisation reduces postoperative complications.
Delayed gastric emptying — treat all decompensated patients as full-stomach for RSI.
Pharmacology in Hepatic Impairment
→ ↑free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs (thiopentone, diazepam, phenytoin).
↑Volume of distribution
from ascites and oedema → larger loading dose for water-soluble drugs (e.g. neuromuscular blockers).
Reduced hepatic clearance
→ prolonged elimination of midazolam, morphine, vecuronium, rocuronium, lidocaine, paracetamol.
↓Plasma cholinesterase
→ variable prolongation of suxamethonium and mivacurium; usually not clinically significant for a single dose.
Portosystemic shunting
→ ↑bioavailability of orally administered, high first-pass drugs (β-blockers, opioids, midazolam).
Practical Drug Choices
: propofol induction dose reduced by
in severe disease (increased volume of distribution, reduced protein binding raising free fraction, and increased receptor sensitivity from encephalopathy) with slow titration to effect; TCI models are not validated in cirrhosis, so use processed EEG monitoring instead
Volatile maintenance
: sevoflurane (~3% metabolism) or desflurane (<0.02%) — both preserve hepatic blood flow;
halothane contraindicated
(immune-mediated halothane hepatitis).
: single fentanyl doses are safe (unchanged clearance for a bolus), but infusions accumulate through reduced hepatic blood flow and clearance;
remifentanil is the opioid of choice
as plasma/tissue esterase metabolism is organ-independent; morphine's half-life roughly doubles and its active metabolites accumulate further if renal function is also impaired; avoid codeine (unreliable CYP2D6 activation) and pethidine
Neuromuscular blockade
: rocuronium's duration of action can double (~45 min extending to ~90 min) because of biliary excretion and a larger volume of distribution — quantitative train-of-four monitoring is mandatory and sugammadex reversal should be available; vecuronium and pancuronium are similarly prolonged;
cisatracurium is the agent of choice
as organ-independent Hofmann elimination is unaffected by hepatic function; suxamethonium may be modestly prolonged by reduced plasma cholinesterase synthesis
: paracetamol is safe at reduced dose in established stable cirrhosis — maximum 2 g/day in severe cirrhosis (or 3 g/day for short courses in mild disease per local guidance) — but avoid in acute liver failure, decompensation, active alcoholic hepatitis and malnutrition, where glutathione stores are depleted;
avoid NSAIDs
(renal and variceal bleeding risk); regional techniques where coagulation allows.
: reduce benzodiazepine dosing — impaired clearance and increased cerebral sensitivity (encephalopathy) markedly prolong effect.
Intraoperative Management
: minimum AAGBI plus arterial line and CVP/IBP for any major or non-trivial surgery; cardiac output monitoring (oesophageal Doppler / LiDCO) for major fluid shifts.
Vascular access
: large-bore peripheral and central access; blood/products available — group-and-save at minimum, cross-match for any abdominal surgery.
Haemodynamic targets
: MAP within 20% of baseline (typically ≥ 65–70 mmHg, ≥ 80 mmHg in HRS); noradrenaline first-line vasopressor; vasopressin/terlipressin for refractory splanchnic vasodilatation.
: lung-protective (V
6 mL/kg IBW, PEEP 5–8); avoid high airway pressures that further reduce hepatic venous outflow.
: balanced crystalloid; 20% albumin for large-volume paracentesis (8 g per litre drained) and HRS; avoid starches; restrict 0.9% saline (hyperchloraemic acidosis worsens AKI).
Temperature & glucose
: actively warm (cirrhotics lose heat rapidly through ascites); monitor glucose — hypoglycaemia common from impaired gluconeogenesis.
Perioperative Decompensation
Patient-Associated Risk Factors
Severity of liver disease
— Child-Pugh class and MELD/MELD-Na are the strongest single predictors; 30-day mortality rises from ~10% (CP-A / MELD < 10) to > 70% (CP-C / MELD > 20) for major abdominal surgery
Clinically significant portal hypertension
— HVPG > 10 mmHg, varices, splenomegaly, ascites; independently doubles perioperative mortality even at lower MELD scores
Active decompensation in the preceding 3 months
— recent variceal bleed, SBP, HRS-AKI or grade III–IV encephalopathy markedly increases risk of recurrence under surgical stress
Hyponatraemia (Na < 130 mmol/L)
— captured in MELD-Na; reflects advanced splanchnic vasodilatation and predicts AKI, encephalopathy and death.
Sarcopenia and frailty
— independent predictors of postoperative mortality beyond MELD; assessed by L3 psoas index, hand-grip strength or Liver Frailty Index
Concurrent infection
— SBP, UTI or cellulitis at the time of surgery is one of the most consistent precipitants of acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF).
Cardiopulmonary comorbidity
— cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension (mPAP > 35 mmHg) substantially increase intraoperative haemodynamic instability and postoperative organ failure.
Renal dysfunction
— baseline creatinine > 133 µmol/L or recent HRS doubles 30-day mortality (captured by both MELD and VOCAL-Penn).
— active alcohol use, untreated hepatitis B/C, and NASH with metabolic syndrome are each associated with higher decompensation rates; abstinence and antiviral therapy before elective surgery measurably reduce risk
Age > 70, ASA ≥ III, BMI extremes
— non-hepatic factors that are integrated into the VOCAL-Penn calculator alongside liver-specific variables
Procedure-Associated Risk Factors
— emergency surgery carries a 2–4-fold increase in perioperative mortality compared with the same operation performed electively, at every MELD/Child-Pugh stratum
Site and type of surgery
— highest risk: open abdominal (especially hepatic resection, colectomy, ulcer surgery), cardiac and trauma surgery; intermediate risk: orthopaedic, vascular, upper GI; lowest risk: superficial, ophthalmic and short laparoscopic procedures
Open vs laparoscopic
— laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hernia repair have lower decompensation rates than open equivalents in compensated cirrhosis, provided pneumoperitoneum is kept ≤ 12 mmHg to preserve hepatic venous outflow.
Duration and blood loss
— operations > 4 h and intraoperative transfusion > 2 units RBC are independent predictors of postoperative ACLF.
Hepatic resection or vascular inflow occlusion
— Pringle manoeuvre and major hepatectomy further reduce functional liver mass; safe future liver remnant ≥ 40% in cirrhosis (vs ≥ 25% in normal liver).
Cardiopulmonary bypass
— non-pulsatile flow, hypothermia, transfusion and systemic inflammation produce a particularly high rate of postoperative liver failure in cirrhosis; off-pump techniques preferred where feasible.
Intra-abdominal surgery in the presence of ascites
— wound dehiscence, infection and incisional hernia rates are substantially higher; consider preoperative paracentesis or TIPSS in selected patients.
Anaesthetic insults
— sustained hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg for > 10 min), high PEEP, high intra-abdominal pressure and hepatotoxic drug exposure (halothane, paracetamol overdose, NSAIDs) precipitate ischaemic hepatic injury.
Risk Stratification Tools
— historic standard; still useful for bedside triage but limited by subjective components and absence of renal function
MELD / MELD-Na
— better continuous predictor; MELD > 15 should trigger formal multidisciplinary review before elective non-transplant surgery.
Mayo Postoperative Mortality Risk Score
— integrates age, MELD, ASA and aetiology to give 7-/30-/90-day mortality estimates (Mayo Clinic online calculator)
— preferred contemporary score in the US/EU; outperforms MELD-Na and Mayo, particularly in compensated patients and laparoscopic procedures
CLIF-C ACLF / CLIF-SOFA
— used postoperatively to grade severity and prognosis if decompensation develops
Strategies to Mitigate Decompensation Risk
Defer non-essential elective surgery if MELD > 15 or Child-Pugh C; transfer high-risk cases to a transplant centre where surgery and post-op liver support are co-located
Treat ongoing precipitants before theatre: alcohol abstinence (≥ 6 weeks where possible), antiviral therapy for HBV/HCV, weight loss in NASH, optimisation of diabetes.
Optimise ascites (low-sodium diet, diuretics, large-volume paracentesis with 8 g albumin per litre drained); consider preoperative TIPSS in refractory ascites or recurrent variceal bleeding before elective abdominal surgery.
Screen for and band-ligate high-risk varices; continue non-selective β-blocker (carvedilol or propranolol) up to surgery, holding only if MAP cannot be maintained.
Treat hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose ± rifaximin to West Haven 0 before elective surgery
Correct hyponatraemia slowly (≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Nutritional pre-habilitation: 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day protein, late-evening snack, branched-chain amino acid supplementation in sarcopenic patients.
Document baseline coagulation with fibrinogen and viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM); avoid prophylactic FFP and platelets — correct only if active bleeding or planned neuraxial
Vaccinate (pneumococcal, influenza, HBV) and treat any active infection — including SBP — before elective surgery.
Multidisciplinary preoperative review (hepatology, anaesthesia, surgery, ITU) with explicit ceiling-of-care discussion documented.
Prefer regional or hybrid techniques where coagulation permits to limit GA and opioid exposure.
Maintain MAP within 20% of baseline (≥ 65–70 mmHg, ≥ 80 mmHg if HRS) with noradrenaline first-line; vasopressin/terlipressin for refractory splanchnic vasodilatation
Lung-protective ventilation with the lowest effective PEEP to preserve hepatic venous outflow; keep intra-abdominal pressure ≤ 12 mmHg for laparoscopy.
Balanced crystalloid and 20% albumin for volume replacement; restrict 0.9% saline and avoid starches.
Viscoelastic-guided product use; tranexamic acid for hyperfibrinolysis; fibrinogen concentrate if FIBTEM A10 < 8 mm; platelets only if < 50 × 10⁹/L with active bleeding
Hepatic-friendly pharmacology: propofol (reduced dose), sevoflurane/desflurane, fentanyl or remifentanil, cisatracurium, paracetamol ≤ 2–3 g/24 h, no NSAIDs.
Active warming and glucose monitoring (hypoglycaemia from impaired gluconeogenesis).
Surgical mitigation: minimise blood loss, avoid Pringle manoeuvre > 30 min in cirrhosis, consider intraoperative cell salvage where appropriate.
HDU or ICU disposition for any MELD > 10 or major surgery; daily review for ascites, encephalopathy, AKI and infection.
Early enteral nutrition; continue lactulose/rifaximin; avoid sedatives and benzodiazepines.
Early VTE prophylaxis (mechanical immediately, pharmacological once haemostasis confirmed) — cirrhosis does
protect against VTE
Vigilance for postoperative sepsis and SBP — low threshold for diagnostic paracentesis and empirical antibiotics with 20% albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3)
Early identification of ACLF using CLIF-SOFA; escalate to transplant centre if grade ≥ 2 with extrahepatic organ failure.
Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF)
: acute decompensation of chronic liver disease (with or without previously diagnosed cirrhosis) producing hepatic failure (jaundice and coagulopathy) plus one or more extrahepatic organ failures, with a 28-day mortality of at least 15%; distinct from simple decompensation, and characterised by systemic inflammation (raised white cell count and CRP, high cytokines) with immune paresis
: EASL-CLIF Consortium definition from the CANONIC study, using CLIF-SOFA/CLIF-C organ failure definitions across six systems — liver (bilirubin ≥ 205 µmol/L), kidney (creatinine ≥ 177 µmol/L or RRT), brain (West Haven grade III–IV encephalopathy), coagulation (INR ≥ 2.5), circulation (vasopressor requirement) and respiration (PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200 or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 214)
: Grade 1 — single renal failure, or single non-renal organ failure with renal dysfunction (creatinine 133–176 µmol/L) or grade I–II encephalopathy (28-day mortality ~20%); Grade 2 — two organ failures (~30–35%); Grade 3 — three or more organ failures (~75%, > 90% with four or more).
: bacterial and fungal sepsis (especially SBP), active alcohol excess, acute viral hepatitis or hepatitis B flare, variceal haemorrhage, drug-induced injury, and surgery.
: early recognition and CLIF-C ACLF scoring; prompt discussion with a specialist hepatology/transplant centre; aggressive search for and treatment of the precipitant (broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h for suspected sepsis, antivirals, alcohol withdrawal management); organ support (noradrenaline with terlipressin/albumin for circulatory failure, RRT, lung-protective ventilation, ammonia-directed management of encephalopathy); enteral nutrition with 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day protein; early assessment for liver transplantation, with reassessment of futility at 3–7 days since failure to improve by day 7 predicts very high mortality
Variceal Haemorrhage — Exact Management
: restrictive transfusion strategy, target
Hb 70–80 g/L
(over-transfusion raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding); permissive hypotension targeting
MAP ~65 mmHg
with lactate clearance as an endpoint; correct hypocalcaemia; avoid excessive crystalloid; correct thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy only if actively bleeding
Splanchnic vasoconstriction
terlipressin 2 mg IV bolus, then 1–2 mg IV 4-hourly
for 2–5 days; watch for hyponatraemia, peripheral and myocardial ischaemia; octreotide/somatostatin are alternatives
Prophylactic antibiotics
: IV ceftriaxone 1 g once daily for up to 7 days in every cirrhotic with GI bleeding — reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality
: within 12 h with
band ligation as first-line
; injection sclerotherapy or glue (cyanoacrylate for gastric varices) second-line
Airway protection
: RSI with a cuffed endotracheal tube before endoscopy in active haematemesis, reduced consciousness or massive bleeding — full-stomach and aspiration precautions; large-bore IV access, blood/platelets available in theatre, vasopressor support ready, active warming, and correction of coagulopathy guided by viscoelastic testing rather than INR alone.
Refractory bleeding — balloon tamponade
: Sengstaken–Blakemore/Minnesota tube in an intubated patient as a bridge for no more than 24 h — confirm gastric balloon position radiographically before full inflation, inflate the gastric balloon (usually 250–500 mL air) and apply traction, use the oesophageal balloon only if bleeding persists and deflate it intermittently; complications include oesophageal rupture, mucosal pressure necrosis, aspiration and airway obstruction on displacement; self-expanding covered oesophageal metal stents are an alternative with lower complication rates.
Rescue therapy
: TIPSS for failed endoscopic control; pre-emptive ("early") TIPSS within 72 h (ideally 24 h) in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C 10–13, or Child-Pugh B with active bleeding at endoscopy) improves survival; contraindications include severe hepatic encephalopathy, heart failure and pulmonary hypertension
Sepsis & Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
Common perioperative precipitant of decompensation; diagnostic paracentesis (ascitic PMN > 250/mm³) for any new clinical change.
Empirical cefotaxime or piperacillin–tazobactam; add 20% albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) — reduces HRS and mortality.
Portal Hypertension Assessment & TIPSS
Hepatic Venous Pressure Gradient (HVPG)
Gold-standard invasive measurement (wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure) of portal pressure.
> 5 mmHg
— portal hypertension present (normal 1–5 mmHg).
> 10 mmHg
— "clinically significant portal hypertension" (CSPH): threshold for varices, ascites, and decompensation; independently doubles perioperative mortality even at lower MELD scores
> 12 mmHg
— threshold above which oesophageal varices bleed; non-selective β-blockade or band ligation reduces HVPG and bleeding risk below this level
HVPG is rarely available outside specialist hepatology centres — non-invasive surrogates are used for risk stratification pre-anaesthesia.
Non-Invasive Surrogates
Platelet count
: < 150 × 10⁹/L raises suspicion of portal hypertension (splenic sequestration); < 100 × 10⁹/L combined with splenomegaly is a strong predictor of varices.
Transient elastography (FibroScan)
: liver stiffness > 20–25 kPa strongly predicts CSPH; combined with platelet count and spleen size (Baveno VI/VII criteria: liver stiffness < 15 kPa and platelets > 150 × 10⁹/L) can safely rule out high-risk varices and avoid screening endoscopy.
Imaging signs of portal hypertension: splenomegaly, portosystemic collaterals, recanalised umbilical vein, ascites on ultrasound/CT.
These surrogates are used preoperatively to flag patients who need OGD variceal screening and closer perioperative haemodynamic control before elective surgery.
TIPSS In Situ — Anaesthetic Implications
A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt decompresses portal pressure and reduces variceal bleeding and refractory ascites, but shunts portal blood directly into the systemic circulation.
Hepatic encephalopathy
occurs or worsens in up to 30–50% after TIPSS (loss of hepatic first-pass clearance of gut-derived ammonia and toxins) — heightened sensitivity to sedatives, opioids and benzodiazepines.
Reduced hepatic synthetic reserve may become apparent post-TIPSS as portal flow to the liver falls — anticipate a worse coagula

# Renal Co-Existing Disease CKD staging, dialysis-dependent patients, altered pharmacology, electrolyte emergencies, transplant recipients, perioperative AKI prevention Step-by-step reasoning Common traps Dialysing the same day as surgery — risks intraoperative hypotension from residual hypovolaemia and heparin-related bleeding. Using the fistula arm for cannulation or NIBP cuff — risks thrombosis of a life-sustaining access. Choosing morphine for analgesia — accumulates active metabolites and precipitates prolonged sedation/respiratory depression. Giving Hartmann's/potassium-containing fluid freely without checking recent potassium. calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV (or calcium gluconate 30 mL 10% if only peripheral access) over 2–5 minutes, repeated if ECG changes persist after 5 minutes — does not lower potassium but stabilises the myocardium. insulin 10 units (Actrapid) in 25 g glucose IV (50 mL 50% glucose or 250 mL 10% glucose) over 15–30 minutes, plus nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg ; monitor capillary glucose for at least 4–6 hours after (risk of delayed hypoglycaemia). Using suxamethonium for RSI in known hyperkalaemia — can precipitate cardiac arrest. Forgetting glucose monitoring after insulin/dextrose — delayed hypoglycaemia is common. Relying on bicarbonate alone as definitive treatment — it is an adjunct, not a substitute for insulin/dextrose or dialysis. Delaying a life-saving laparotomy purely to "normalise" potassium — treat in parallel, not sequentially. CKD Staging & Uraemic Multi-System Effects KDIGO/NICE CKD Classification eGFR categories : G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73m² (or established renal replacement therapy) Albuminuria categories (ACR): A1 <3 mg/mmol, A2 3–30 mg/mmol, A3 >30 mg/mmol. CKD is defined as abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for >3 months; combining eGFR and albuminuria categories on a "heat-map" predicts progression and cardiovascular mortality risk Prevalence in the surgical population is high and frequently unrecognised — routine preoperative U&E should prompt eGFR calculation in at-risk groups (diabetes, hypertension, age >60, vascular disease). Uraemic Multi-System Effects : reduced erythropoietin production plus iron-restricted erythropoiesis; target Hb 100–120 g/L on ESA therapy — over-correction increases thrombotic and cardiovascular risk. Platelet dysfunction : uraemic toxins impair platelet–vessel wall adhesion (abnormal bleeding time) despite a normal platelet count and standard coagulation screen; bleeding risk is clinically significant and not detected by INR/APTT. Autonomic neuropathy : blunted baroreceptor reflexes cause labile blood pressure and an exaggerated hypotensive response to induction agents, neuraxial blockade and fluid shifts. Accelerated cardiovascular disease : CKD is a coronary heart disease risk-equivalent — accelerated atherosclerosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, vascular calcification and high rates of silent ischaemia. Renal bone disease (CKD-MBD) : secondary hyperparathyroidism, hyperphosphataemia, vascular calcification and osteodystrophy — relevant to positioning (fracture risk) and airway/spine considerations. Delayed gastric emptying : autonomic neuropathy and uraemia slow gastric emptying — treat advanced CKD/dialysis patients as at increased aspiration risk and consider rapid sequence induction for emergency surgery Preoperative Assessment & Optimisation Timing of Dialysis Elective haemodialysis should ideally occur the day before surgery , aiming for dry (or near-dry) weight and correction of biochemistry, rather than same-day dialysis which risks residual heparinisation and volume shifts Aim for a pre-theatre serum potassium <5.5 mmol/L before elective surgery; recheck U&E on the day of surgery. Peritoneal dialysis patients should drain the abdomen before surgery (especially abdominal/laparoscopic procedures) and may need a temporary switch to haemodialysis or reduced dwell volumes perioperatively. Fistula Protection No blood pressure cuffs, venepuncture, cannulation or arterial lines in the fistula limb — clearly label the notes, theatre door and the limb itself. Avoid prolonged pressure or awkward positioning of the fistula arm during surgery; check for a palpable thrill/audible bruit before and after the case. Anaemia, Antihypertensives and Nephrotoxin Avoidance Continue iron and erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) therapy; correct significant anaemia before major elective surgery, avoiding unnecessary transfusion which risks HLA sensitisation and reduces future transplant compatibility. ACE inhibitors/ARBs : consider omitting on the morning of surgery for major/intermediate-risk surgery to reduce refractory intraoperative hypotension, particularly with neuraxial or general anaesthesia and significant fluid shifts. SGLT2 inhibitors ("sick day rules"): stop 3 days before major surgery (2 days for ertugliflozin/dapagliflozin per some protocols) due to the risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis and perioperative AKI Avoid iodinated and other nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs) in the perioperative period in patients with residual renal function; if contrast unavoidable, ensure euvolaemia and use the lowest effective dose. Pharmacology in Renal Impairment Neuromuscular Blockade Atracurium and cisatracurium are preferred — Hofmann elimination and non-specific ester hydrolysis are organ-independent, giving predictable duration in renal failure. # Gastrointestinal Co-Existing Disease
GORD and aspiration risk, inflammatory bowel disease, malnutrition, intestinal failure, bowel obstruction and stoma physiology

Step-by-step reasoning
Common traps
Assuming standard fasting times protect against aspiration — achalasia empties by gravity, not peristalsis, and residue can remain despite prolonged starvation.
Relying on metoclopramide to "empty" an aperistaltic oesophagus.
Extubating deep to avoid coughing on the tube — removes airway protection at the point of highest regurgitation risk.
Withholding VTE prophylaxis because of rectal bleeding — active IBD is strongly prothrombotic and mechanical + pharmacological prophylaxis should continue.
Forgetting stress-dose steroids in a patient on recent high-dose corticosteroids — risk of adrenal crisis.
Delaying surgery to "optimise" a patient who has already failed medical rescue therapy — toxic megacolon/perforation risk rises with delay.
