# Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry Redox reactions, electrode potentials, clinical electrodes, free radicals transfer of electrons between species. They are fundamental to energy metabolism (electron transport chain), drug metabolism (cytochrome P450), clinical measurement (Clark and Severinghaus electrodes), and pathology (free radical injury). OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. The species that loses electrons is and acts as the reducing agent ; the species that gains electrons is oxidising agent standard electrode potential (E⁰) of a half-reaction is measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂, defined as E⁰ = 0.0 V) under standard conditions (298 K, 1 atm, 1 M concentration). A positive E⁰ indicates a strong oxidising agent (high affinity for electrons); a negative E⁰ indicates a strong reducing agent (tends to donate electrons). O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O: E⁰ = +1.23 V (standard conditions); falls to ≈ +0.82 V at pH 7 because the Nernst equation is H⁺-dependent Cytochrome c (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺): E⁰ ≈ +0.25 V NAD⁺/NADH: E⁰ = −0.32 V (strong reducing couple) Nernst equation , E = E⁰ − (RT/nF)lnQ, describes how the actual electrode potential varies with the concentration (activity) of reactants and products (Q) around the standard value, where R is the gas constant, T absolute temperature, n the number of electrons transferred, and F the Faraday constant. This concentration-dependence is the working principle of ion-selective electrodes (pH glass electrode, Na⁺/K⁺ electrodes) and explains why electrode readings shift predictably with analyte concentration rather than being fixed. oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ . MetHb cannot bind oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve of remaining HbO₂ to the left, worsening tissue hypoxia. Common precipitants: prilocaine, benzocaine, dapsone, GTN, sulphonamides, and inhaled nitric oxide methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV (acts via NADPH–methaemoglobin reductase). Methylene blue is itself an oxidiser at high doses and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — use ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion instead. Clark electrode (PO₂) : amperometric. A polarising voltage (~0.6 V) is applied between a platinum cathode and a silver/silver-chloride anode in KCl electrolyte. O₂ diffuses through a polypropylene membrane and is reduced at the cathode; the resulting current is proportional to PO₂. Severinghaus electrode (PCO₂) : CO₂ diffuses across a Teflon membrane into a thin film of sodium bicarbonate solution, forming carbonic acid and lowering the pH. The pH change is measured by a glass electrode and converted to PCO₂. Galvanic (fuel) cell : a self-contained battery-like O₂ analyser used for the constant-threshold O₂ alarm on the anaesthetic machine backbar. It generates a current proportional to pO₂ without needing any external polarising voltage — the chemical reaction itself is the power source. A lead anode gold cathode sit in a potassium hydroxide (KOH) electrolyte: at the anode, Pb + 2OH⁻ → PbO + H₂O + 2e⁻; at the cathode, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Because the lead anode is progressively consumed, cell lifespan is finite — typically 1–2 years , and cells are rated in ampere-hours (or "oxygen-hours") of remaining life. Response is relatively slow (~ 20 s ), but there is no calibration drift over the short term, making it well suited to constant-threshold alarm duty rather than breath-by-breath analysis. polarographic (Clark) electrode requires an externally applied polarising voltage (~ 600 mV ) to drive O₂ reduction at its platinum cathode. It responds faster but is prone to calibration drift and membrane fouling, requiring more frequent recalibration than the galvanic cell. Ion-selective electrodes (ISE) : an ion-specific membrane — glass for H⁺/Na⁺, valinomycin for K⁺, or an ion-exchange resin for Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ — develops a potential difference across it that is described by the , measured against a reference electrode under zero-current ( ) conditions. ISEs measure ion , not concentration, so results are affected by protein and lipid content in the sample; measuring with an ISE on a blood gas analyser avoids the seen with indirect, diluted flame-photometric methods in samples with high protein or lipid content. Glucose sensor : amperometric. Glucose oxidase oxidises glucose to gluconolactone, generating hydrogen peroxide ; the H₂O₂ is then oxidised at a polarised platinum anode (~ +0.6 V ), producing a current proportional to glucose concentration — a Clark-type cell arrangement. Readings can be affected by interfering substances such as paracetamol, ascorbate and icodextrin superoxide (O₂⁻·), hydroxyl radical (OH·) and peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) . Endogenous antioxidants — superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione, and dietary vitamins C and E — keep ROS in check. Oxygen toxicity : hyperoxia drives excess mitochondrial and enzymatic production of superoxide (O₂⁻·) , which is dismutated to and then, via iron-catalysed Fenton and Haber-Weiss chemistry, to the highly reactive hydroxyl radical (OH·) . Oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions involve the transfer of electrons between species. They are fundamental to energy metabolism (electron transport chain), drug metabolism (cytochrome P450), clinical measurement (Clark and Severinghaus electrodes), and pathology (free radical injury).

Remember OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. The species that loses electrons is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent; the species that gains electrons is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.
